cards.try_team: Everyone writes one goal for this term on a card and swaps with a partner, who checks in weekly: 'Still your goal? What's the next step?'

cards.hook: Played guitar for 10 years? Why might year 10 feel like year 2?
cards.title: Deliberate Practice

game.prompt: You've got 10 minutes with your guitar. What order levels you up?
items: Pick the bit you always mess up
Do just that bit, slightly too hard
Check what went wrong, then go again
game.explain: Pick the bit you always mess up → do just that bit, slightly too hard → check what went wrong, then go again. Songs you know keep your skill and your joy, but mostly hold you where you are.

cards.insight: Hours alone don't make experts; focused work on weak spots helps far more. The '10,000-hour rule' oversimplifies Ericsson, and a 2014 meta-analysis found practice explains only part of skill gaps.
cards.model: For growth, not more practice: narrower, slightly too hard, with feedback. Keep playing for joy too.
cards.try_today: Pick a skill you use often, name its weakest sub-part, and drill only that for 10 focused minutes.

source.work: Peak (2016); Deliberate practice and performance: a meta-analysis (2014)

cards.try_team: Pick one thing your team, class or family does often (a pitch, a dish, a match). Name its weakest part and run 3 quick rounds on just that, with feedback.

cards.hook: You've played one game for 500 hours. Are you actually getting better?
cards.title: Practice or Just Repetition?

game.prompt: Does this grow the skill, or just keep it where it is?

items.text: Playing ranked matches every night without ever watching your replays.
items.why: Hours on autopilot keep your rank where it is. Replays show the exact mistake.

items.text: Replaying the 3 bars you always fumble, slowly, until they're clean.
items.why: One weak spot, just past your level, with instant feedback from your own ears. Textbook.

items.text: Driving to work every day for 20 years.
items.why: Keeps you fluent, but rarely sharpens skills like skid control. That needs targeted practice.

items.text: Going back over a chess game you lost to find the move where it went wrong.
items.why: Finding the exact error and fixing it is the heart of deliberate practice.

items.text: A 400-day streak on a language app, always on the easy setting.
items.why: Streaks build habit, which matters. But if it never stretches you, it's mostly upkeep.

items.text: Rewriting a great article from your notes, then comparing it to the original.
items.why: Ben Franklin's own trick: the original shows exactly where your version falls short.

items.text: Cooking a new dish, then asking someone for one thing to change.
items.why: A stretch plus honest feedback. Asking for just one thing keeps it usable.

cards.insight: Ericsson argued extra hours add little once a skill feels automatic; growth needs narrow, slightly-too-hard work with feedback. Practice matters, but less than he claimed (Macnamara, 2014).
cards.model: Hours keep a skill. Feedback on your weakest part grows it.
cards.try_today: Pick a hobby where you've stopped improving. Find the one moment you always get wrong and practise only that for 10 minutes.
cards.try_team: Pick one thing your class, team or family does on repeat. Ask: where are we just repeating? Choose one weak spot to practise, with feedback.

source.work: Peak (2016); The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (1791); Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald, Psychological Science (2014)

from_source.quote: without looking at the book, try'd to compleat the papers again
from_source.cite: Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography, Part One (written 1771), on rewriting Spectator essays
from_source.next_read: Franklin's Autobiography, Part One: the passage where he teaches himself to write from The Spectator

cards.hook: You just messed up in front of people. What you do next matters.
cards.title: Mistakes as Data

steps.scenario: You posted the wrong date for a friend's party in the group chat. Two people already planned around it. Someone points it out. Your first move…

options.text: Quietly delete the message and hope nobody noticed.
options.feedback: Very human. But the lesson stays hidden, and people may still plan around the wrong date.

options.text: Post a short correction: what was wrong, the right date, sorry for the hassle.
options.feedback: Clean and calm. Owning it fast builds trust and stops the error spreading.

options.text: Apologise at length about how useless you are.
options.feedback: Harsh self-talk feels responsible but uses energy you need for the fix. Be kind to yourself and precise about the error.

steps.scenario: That evening the mistake is still on your mind. What do you do with it?

options.text: Replay it and feel bad until it fades.
options.feedback: Understandable, but feeling bad isn't the same as learning. The pain is a signal, not the lesson.

options.text: Write 3 lines: what happened, why, what I'll change.
options.feedback: This is the alchemy: a mistake turned into a rule you keep, like 'check the date before I post'.

options.text: Decide you're just hopeless at organising things.
options.feedback: One slip is one data point, not a verdict on you. Look for the cause you can change.

cards.insight: A mistake shows exactly where your method breaks. Ray Dalio sums it up as pain plus reflection equals progress. The trick is to study the cause, not punish yourself.
cards.model: Mistake → cause → new rule. Keep the lesson, drop the shame.
cards.try_today: Write down one recent mistake in 3 lines: what happened, why, and one rule you'll follow next time.

source.work: Principles: Life and Work (2017)

cards.try_team: After a slip at work, school or home, hold a 5-minute no-blame review: what happened, why, and one rule you add. Talk about the process, not the person.

from_source.quote: To have faults and not to reform them, this, indeed, should be pronounced having faults.
from_source.cite: Confucius, Analects XV.29 (trans. James Legge, 1861)
from_source.next_read: Analects, Book I.8 ('When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them') and Book XV

cards.hook: What makes a good day at work or study? Bosses guessed wrong.
cards.title: The Progress Principle

game.prompt: 669 managers ranked five things that motivate people: praise, rewards, clear goals, support, and making progress. Where did 'making progress' land?
game.reveal: Dead last. Yet in nearly 12,000 diary entries from 238 workers, making progress on meaningful work was the strongest booster of their best days. Same goes for school: a tiny visible win beats a big vague goal.

cards.insight: We underrate small steps, yet in 12,000 diary entries visible progress lifted motivation most. Keeping a record of your wins gives you evidence to reach for on hard days.
cards.model: Progress you can see is the strongest fuel. Keep evidence of it.
cards.try_today: Start a 'wins' note: list 3 hard things you've already handled. Add one small win every evening.

source.work: The Progress Principle (2011)

cards.try_team: End a meeting, class or family dinner with one quick round: 'One small step forward I made this week.' 30 seconds each, no ranking.

cards.hook: One step forward, one step back. Which does your brain count louder?
cards.title: Setbacks Shout, Wins Whisper

game.prompt: In a diary study, 238 people wrote about their workday, every day, for months. What moved their mood more: a step forward, or a step back?
game.reveal: A step back. In Amabile and Kramer's diaries, a setback's power to sink happiness was more than twice as strong as progress's power to lift it. If you picked 'forward', that's the hopeful guess, and progress did matter a lot. It just whispers while setbacks shout.

cards.insight: Bad events tend to weigh more than good ones (Baumeister and colleagues, 2001). So a day with one step forward and one back can feel like a loss. Writing wins down gives them a fair vote.
cards.model: Setbacks shout, progress whispers. Write the wins down so they get a vote.
cards.try_today: Tonight, write one step back and two steps forward from today, however small. Read the forward ones twice.
cards.try_team: End the week with each person naming one setback and one bit of progress. Write the progress where everyone can see it.

source.work: The Progress Principle (2011); Bad is stronger than good (2001)

cards.hook: Is this the dip you push through, or the sign to walk away?
cards.title: Quitting Wisely

game.prompt: Is this a real quit signal, or not (yet)?

items.text: It's hard, but you're measurably better than a month ago.
items.why: Hard plus progress is the classic dip. The reward usually lies on the other side.

items.text: You keep going mainly because of what you've already spent.
items.why: That's the sunk cost trap. Past costs are gone either way; judge only the road ahead.

items.text: Knowing what you know now, you'd never start this today.
items.why: Annie Duke's test: if you wouldn't choose it fresh, staying is often just inertia.

items.text: You had a terrible week and feel like giving up tonight.
items.why: Your feeling is real and worth hearing. One bad night just isn't enough to decide on. Rest first.

items.text: Your goal changed and this no longer leads anywhere you want.
items.why: Grit toward the wrong goal is just stubbornness. Redirect the effort.

items.text: It keeps costing you sleep, health, or key relationships.
items.why: Real harm is a stop sign, not a toughness test. Protect the base everything else is built on.

items.text: You're stuck, but you haven't tried a new method yet.
items.why: Change the approach before the goal. Stuck is often a method problem.

cards.insight: Quitting isn't failure; it frees time for better bets. Seth Godin separates a dip worth pushing through from a dead end. Annie Duke adds: we usually quit too late, held by sunk costs.
cards.model: Quit what you wouldn't start today. Dips that still show progress aren't quit signals.
cards.try_today: Write one commitment you're unsure about and set a 'stop signal': the one sign that would tell you to stop.

source.work: Quit (2022); The Dip (2007)

cards.try_team: Pick one shared project, club or family plan and agree its stop signals together: 'If ___ hasn't happened by ___, we stop or change course.'

cards.hook: Kids once got around town alone. How fast did that freedom shrink?
cards.title: The Shrinking Roam

game.question: In 1971, 80% of English 7- and 8-year-olds got to school without an adult. By 1990, what share did?
game.explain: 9%. In under 20 years, going to school alone fell from 8 in 10 young kids to fewer than 1 in 10 (Hillman, Adams & Whitelegg, 1990). Busier roads and parents' fears grew; kids' chances to handle small risks on their own shrank.

cards.insight: The drop is real. Haidt and Gray link it to rising teen anxiety; critics say the evidence is mostly correlation. Either way, small risks you choose seem to build skill and nerve.
cards.model: Nerve grows from small risks you choose and can judge yourself, at any age.
cards.try_today: Pick one small thing you'd usually hand to someone else, a new route, a repair, a tricky call, and do it yourself today.
cards.try_team: Each person names one thing they did alone at 10 that kids rarely do now. Agree one safe-enough version to allow or try this month.

source.work: One False Move: A Study of Children's Independent Mobility (1990); Gray, The Decline of Play (2011); Haidt, The Anxious Generation (2024)

cards.hook: Mates jumping off a pier. Brave or daft? There's a third option.
cards.title: Keep the Risk, Fix the Hazard

steps.scenario: Your friends are jumping off a pier into water nobody has checked. Your move?

options.text: Check the depth first, then decide.
options.feedback: Best pick. Unknown depth is a hazard: a danger you can't see. Make it visible, then the choice is really yours.

options.text: Jump. Hesitating is for cowards.
options.feedback: Courage isn't skipping the check. Hidden rocks don't care how brave you are.

options.text: Never jump, from any pier, ever.
options.feedback: Safe tonight, but avoiding every risk builds fear, not skill. Check first, then choose.

steps.scenario: Your 7-year-old cousin is climbing a sturdy tree, a little higher than you'd like. You call up…

options.text: "Do you feel steady? Where does your next foot go?"
options.feedback: Best pick. A question hands her the judgment. The height is a risk she can see and manage, the useful kind.

options.text: "Get down now, that's too high!"
options.feedback: Understandable, and it ends the danger. It also ends the lesson: she never practises judging height herself.

options.text: Nothing. You look away and let her get on with it.
options.feedback: Trust is good, but staying near and calm lets you spot what she can't, like a rotten branch.

steps.scenario: Your mate asks to lead the group presentation solo. It feels a bit early for them. You…

options.text: Say yes, run through it once together, and be ready to jump in.
options.feedback: Best pick. Real stakes, a safety net, and room to recover: that's risky play at any age.

options.text: Do it yourself. Too much is riding on it.
options.feedback: Safe for this class, costly for growth. Without a first try, the next one stays scary.

options.text: Let them wing it with no run-through.
options.feedback: That's a hazard, not a stretch: missing facts they can't see. Give the map, then step back.

cards.insight: A risk is a danger you can see and judge; a hazard is one you can't. Fix hazards, keep risks. A 2015 review tied risky outdoor play to more activity and social health; most studies were weak.
cards.model: Remove the hidden hazards, keep the visible risks. That's where skill and courage grow.
cards.try_today: Swap one 'Be careful!' for a question: 'What's your plan?' or 'Do you feel steady?' Try it on a kid, a colleague or yourself.
cards.try_team: At work, class or home, list 3 things you shield people from (a first client call, a solo trip). Sort each: hidden hazard (fix it) or visible risk (allow it).

source.work: Brussoni et al., Risky Play and Children's Safety (2012); Brussoni et al., risky outdoor play and health: a systematic review (2015)

cards.hook: Some mistakes are worth making. Can you spot which?
cards.title: The Useful Kind of Mistake

game.prompt: Two friends each burn dinner. Ana tried a new recipe, in a small batch, noting what she changed. Ben made his usual dish but forgot the timer. Whose mistake teaches more?
game.reveal: Ana's. Amy Edmondson calls it an intelligent failure: new ground, small stakes, a real question answered. Ben's is a basic failure: worth a quick fix (set a timer), but it holds no new lesson.

cards.insight: Mistakes on new ground show you what nobody knew yet. Mistakes on known ground just need a better system. Sort them, and stop feeling equally bad about both.
cards.model: New ground: make small, smart mistakes. Known ground: add a check.
cards.try_today: Think of your last slip. New ground or known ground? Write one small experiment to try, or one check to add.

source.work: Right Kind of Wrong: The Science of Failing Well (2023)

cards.try_team: List 3 recent slips as a team, class or family. Sort each: new ground (share the lesson) or known ground (add a check). No blame.

cards.hook: It went fine. Is that the end of the lesson?
cards.title: The Reflection Loop

steps.scenario: Your team won 3-1, but you missed two easy passes. On the way home you…

options.text: Enjoy the win and forget the rest.
options.feedback: Enjoy it, you earned it. But the misses hold the lesson, and they fade fast.

options.text: Enjoy the win, then name one thing that worked and one pass to practise.
options.feedback: That's the loop: notice, pick one change, try it next time. Wins teach too.

options.text: Replay the two misses all evening.
options.feedback: Caring is good, but replaying isn't reviewing. Name the fix, then let it go.

steps.scenario: You gave a talk at school or work. It went OK but felt flat. The most useful question afterwards is…

options.text: "Was I good or bad?"
options.feedback: That's a verdict, not a lesson. It gives you nothing to change.

options.text: "What's one thing I'll do differently next time?"
options.feedback: Yes. Specific and forward. One change you'll actually try beats ten you won't.

options.text: "Why am I always so boring?"
options.feedback: Harsh and too broad. Swap 'always' for one moment you can fix.

cards.insight: Looking back pays when it ends in one change you'll try next time. Review wins as well as misses, and judge the method, not yourself.
cards.model: Do it, look back, pick one change, try again.
cards.try_today: Tonight, write two lines about today: one thing that worked, and one small thing you'll do differently tomorrow.

source.work: Kolb, Experiential Learning (1984); Schön, The Reflective Practitioner (1983); Seneca, On Anger III.36

cards.try_team: End your next team, class or family task with 5 minutes: what worked, what didn't, one change to try next time. No blame.

from_source.quote: What fault have you resisted? In what respect are you better?
from_source.cite: Seneca, On Anger III.36, quoting Sextius (trans. John W. Basore, 1928)
from_source.next_read: Seneca, On Anger, Book III, ch. 36 (one page)

cards.hook: Your team has a mindset too. Your habits tell people which one.
cards.title: Team Mindset Signals

game.prompt: What does this manager habit teach the team?

items.text: Praising the 'naturals' in every team meeting
items.why: It says ability is handed out, not built. Others stop showing what they can't do yet.

items.text: Asking in stand-up: 'Where did you get stuck?'
items.why: Getting stuck becomes normal and visible, so help arrives before the deadline does.

items.text: Hiring only 'rock stars' who need no training
items.why: It signals that needing to learn is a weakness, even for people already on the team.

items.text: Handing someone a stretch project with weekly check-ins
items.why: Hard work plus support says 'you can grow into this', not 'sink or swim'.

items.text: Writing someone off after one weak quarter
items.why: One rough patch gets treated as a verdict on ability instead of a problem to solve.

items.text: Telling your team about a mistake you made last month
items.why: When the boss admits a gap, everyone else can too. Learning starts at the top.

cards.insight: Verdict: habits beat slogans. Staff at firms seen as 'talent is fixed' reported less trust and more corner-cutting. It's survey data, and mindset effects overall are contested.
cards.model: Teams copy what leaders reward: praise 'naturals' and people hide gaps; praise progress and they share them.
cards.try_today: In your next 1:1, ask 'What's one thing you're finding hard to learn right now?' and thank them for the honest answer.

source.work: Canning et al., Cultures of genius at work, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin (2020); Sisk et al., Psychological Science (2018)

cards.try_team: 5-minute stand-up round: each person names one thing they got stuck on this week and what unstuck it. The manager goes first.

cards.hook: Someone on your team asks how to get better. 'Do more' is the trap.
cards.title: Coach the Weak Spot

steps.scenario: In your 1:1, Sam says: 'I want to get better at client pitches.' Sam has done dozens. You suggest…

options.text: Take every pitch going. Reps make you sharp.
options.feedback: Reps help early on. After that, people often repeat what they already do well. Reps need a target.

options.text: Pick one weak part, like handling price pushback, and rehearse just that with me this week.
options.feedback: Yes. One narrow skill, just past comfort, with fast feedback. That's deliberate practice.

options.text: Shadow our best seller and copy their style.
options.feedback: Good for seeing what great looks like. But Sam won't learn what to change in their own pitch.

steps.scenario: Friday's rehearsal: Sam answers three mock objections from you. Your feedback is…

options.text: "Great job, you sounded really confident!"
options.feedback: Kind, and confidence matters. But Sam leaves with nothing specific to try next time.

options.text: "Your second answer landed because you named their worry first. Try that on the other two, now."
options.feedback: Specific, tied to one move, and retried straight away. That's the loop that builds skill.

options.text: A full list of twelve things to fix.
options.feedback: Thorough and well meant, but too much to act on. One or two changes at a time actually stick.

cards.insight: Verdict: experience alone often plateaus. Rehearsing one weak spot with quick feedback beats more of the same. How much practice explains expertise is contested.
cards.model: Better comes from one weak spot, practised just past comfort, with feedback you can use on the next try.
cards.try_today: Ask one person on your team which single part of their job they'd most like to improve, and book 15 minutes to rehearse it.

source.work: Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer, Psychological Review (1993); Macnamara & Maitra, Royal Society Open Science (2019)

cards.try_team: 5 min in pairs: pick one tricky moment (a client objection, a pushback email). Try it twice; your partner gives one specific note between tries.

cards.hook: Grittier kids went further. Not by trying hard at everything, though.
cards.title: Grit's Secret Weapon

steps.scenario: National spelling bee finalists, aged 7 to 15, prepared three ways. Which one best predicted how far they got?

options.text: Reading books for fun
options.feedback: Great for vocab, and fun matters. But it didn't predict who went further in the bee.

options.text: Being quizzed by family and friends
options.feedback: Fair guess: it's active and social. It predicted progress less well than the option nobody enjoyed.

options.text: Studying hard words alone, on their own weak spots
options.feedback: Yes. Spellers rated it the least fun and most effortful, and it was the best predictor of success.

steps.scenario: Spanish speaking exam in a month. You always freeze on the past tense. Using the spelling bee result, you…

options.text: Chat on Duolingo with mates every evening
options.feedback: Fun, so keep it. But you'll mostly dodge the past tense without noticing.

options.text: Do 15 minutes alone saying past-tense sentences out loud, then do the fun stuff
options.feedback: That's it. Short, boring, aimed at the gap. The fun stuff is your reward and your test.

options.text: Watch Spanish TikToks for slang
options.feedback: Inspiring, and you'll pick up phrases. Your weak spot still needs the reps, though.

cards.insight: Verdict: grit paid off through dull, focused solo practice. Grittier spellers did more of it, and that explained their edge. Grit's wider power is contested: effects are modest.
cards.model: Grit works by getting you to do the boring practice on your weak spot, not by looking busy.
cards.try_today: Pick one weak spot (a topic, a skill, a tense you freeze on) and give it 15 focused minutes alone today, phone in another room.

source.work: Duckworth et al., Deliberate practice spells success, Social Psychological and Personality Science (2011)

cards.try_team: Class or squad, 5 min: everyone writes their one weak spot on a card, does 3 focused minutes on just that, then shares one thing they noticed.

cards.hook: You swear you'll stop scrolling in bed. Why does it never stick?
cards.title: The Habit Loop

steps.scenario: Every night your phone lies on your pillow, and you scroll until 1am. Which change is most likely to break the loop?

options.text: Promise yourself: lights off at 11 tonight.
options.feedback: Worth a try, but it fights the craving head-on, late at night, when you're tired. That's the hardest link to win.

options.text: Charge the phone across the room or outside the bedroom.
options.feedback: Yes. No phone in reach, no cue. You broke the loop at its first link, before willpower was even needed.

options.text: Feel bad about it the next morning.
options.feedback: Guilt arrives after the loop is done, so it changes no link. Be kind to yourself and move the cue instead.

steps.scenario: You're revising. Every time you hit a hard question, your hand goes to your phone. The hard question (the cue) won't vanish. What helps most?

options.text: Delete the app forever.
options.feedback: Big promise, but the urge still has nowhere to go. It usually comes back.

options.text: When a question feels hard, write down the one bit you're stuck on, then try it for 2 minutes.
options.feedback: Yes. Same cue, new response. Swapping in a competing action is the core of habit reversal, a method well tested for tics and nail-biting, and a sensible thing to try here.

options.text: Revise when you feel more motivated.
options.feedback: Understandable, but the loop keeps practising meanwhile. A swap can start today.

cards.insight: Fighting the craving late at night is the hardest link to win. Moving the cue avoids the fight. Clear's loop has four links (Duhigg's had three): remove the cue or swap the response.
cards.model: Cue, craving, response, reward. Change one link and the habit starts to change.
cards.try_today: Pick one habit you want to change and write down its cue. Then move that cue out of sight or out of reach.
cards.try_team: Each person names one group habit (late starts, phones out in meetings or at dinner). Together, name its cue and pick one link to change for a week.

from_source.quote: Could the young but realize how soon they will become mere walking bundles of habits, they would give more heed to their conduct...
from_source.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. IV 'Habit'
from_source.next_read: The Principles of Psychology, ch. IV 'Habit' (the closing pages, with his practical maxims)

source.work: The Power of Habit (2012); Atomic Habits (2018); Habit reversal (Behaviour Research and Therapy, 1973)

cards.hook: Everyone quotes a number for building a habit. It's way off.
cards.title: How Long a Habit Really Takes

game.question: In a UK study, people built one new daily habit. How many days did it take, on median, to feel automatic?
game.explain: Lally and colleagues (2010) followed 96 people for 12 weeks. For the 39 whose data were clear enough to model, the median was 66 days, and the projected range ran from 18 to 254 days. The popular '21 days' has no solid research behind it.

cards.insight: Still effortful after three weeks? That's normal, not failure. Simple habits (a glass of water) automate faster than hard ones (50 sit-ups). Small study, wide range: patience is part of the method.
cards.model: A typical habit took around two months in one small study, and the range is huge. Plan for the long middle.
cards.try_today: Pick one tiny habit and mark a date 66 days from today in your calendar as its check-in day.
cards.try_team: Choose one shared habit (a 5pm tidy-up, a 1-minute check-in). Put a review date 66 days out on the shared calendar and judge it then, not before.

source.work: How are habits formed (European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010)

cards.hook: Same habit, two ways to talk about it. Which one sounds like you?
cards.title: Outcome vs Identity Habits

questions.q: Someone offers you something you're cutting back on (a snack, an energy drink, one more episode). You'd most likely say...

options.label: No thanks, I'm trying to cut down.
No thanks, that's not really me anymore.

questions.q: Your main aim for fitness, study or a hobby sounds most like...

options.label: Hit a number by a date (a grade, 5 km, a weight).
Be someone who does it most days.

questions.q: After a good session, your first thought is usually...

options.label: One step closer to the target.
That's the kind of person I am.

questions.q: On a slow week, what keeps you going?

options.label: Not wanting to stop being who I've become.

zones.label: Leaning outcome today
zones.text: Today's answers aim at results. Great for direction, but results arrive slowly and can feel stuck before they show. Try adding one 'who am I becoming' line.

zones.label: A mix today
zones.text: Today's answers use both. Goals set the direction; identity can keep you going while results are slow.

zones.label: Leaning identity today
zones.text: Today's answers tie actions to who you're becoming. That can make habits sticky. Keep the identity flexible, so one slip never feels like a verdict.

cards.insight: Each small action is a vote for a type of person; you need a majority, not every vote. Clear's idea is a useful lens with little direct testing. Aristotle: we become what we repeatedly do.
cards.model: Every action is a vote for the person you're becoming. Win the majority, not every vote.
cards.try_today: Finish this sentence on paper: 'I am the kind of person who...' Then do one 2-minute action that proves it.
cards.try_team: Each person finishes 'We're the kind of team (or family) that...' Pick the line you like most and one 2-minute action that proves it this week.

from_source.quote: We become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 1 (W. D. Ross trans., 1925)
from_source.next_read: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapters 1-4 (how character is built by repeated action)

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); Nicomachean Ethics (c. 340 BCE)

cards.hook: Can't vote yet? One tiny word might still change what you actually do.
cards.title: The Voter Study That Didn't Hold

game.prompt: Before an election, researchers asked people one of two questions. Which did the FIRST study (2011) report worked better?
choices: How important is it to you to vote?
How important is it to you to be a voter?
game.reveal: The first study (Bryan et al., 2011) said 'be a voter'. Then a bigger study (Gerber et al., 2016) found no effect. The real lesson: one exciting study isn't proof.

cards.insight: Describing an action as part of who you are ('a voter', 'a reader') may make it feel more meaningful. But the original finding did not reliably replicate, so hold it loosely.
cards.model: A catchy finding is a hypothesis until it replicates. Identity labels may help some; test it on yourself.
cards.try_today: Swap "I should revise" for "I'm someone who revises", then revise for 10 minutes. Your own small experiment: does it feel different?
cards.try_team: Rewrite one group rule as a noun: 'be on time' becomes 'we're people who start on time'. Try it for a week, then ask if it felt any different.

source.work: Motivating voter turnout by invoking the self (PNAS, 2011)

cards.hook: 1% a day sounds like nothing. Guess what it compounds to in a year.
cards.title: 1% Compounding

game.question: Something grows 1% a day, compounding, for 365 days. How many times bigger is it at the end?
game.explain: 1.01 to the power of 365 is about 37.8; 1% worse daily (0.99^365) leaves about 0.03. People aren't bank accounts: skills plateau and rest days are part of it. The point is direction, not 37x.

cards.insight: We expect straight-line progress, so small daily gains feel pointless. Real skills plateau and days vary, so this is an illustration, not a forecast. Small choices still add up, both ways.
cards.model: Tiny gains compound. Judge your habits by their direction, not by today's result.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you do daily and make it 1% better today: one more page, one less scroll, one extra glass of water.
cards.try_team: Each person names one 1% fix for how you live or work together (a tidier shared shelf, a shorter meeting). Pick one and do it daily this week.

from_source.quote: Every smallest stroke of virtue or of vice leaves its never so little scar.
from_source.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. IV 'Habit'
from_source.next_read: The Principles of Psychology, ch. IV 'Habit' (the Rip Van Winkle passage near the end)

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); The Principles of Psychology (1890)

cards.hook: 1,000 coins a day for a month, or 1 coin doubling daily? Pick fast.
cards.title: The Doubling Pile

game.prompt: Pick a pile. Pile A: you get 1,000 coins every day for 30 days. Pile B: you get 1 coin on day 1, 2 on day 2, 4 on day 3, doubling each day until day 30. Which ends bigger?
game.reveal: Pile B, by a mile: over 1 billion coins vs 30,000. If you picked A, you're in good company: A is ahead for the first 13 days. Doubling looks like nothing, then like everything.

cards.insight: People reliably underestimate doubling (Stango & Zinman, 2009). Habits don't double: they grow fast, then level off, after 18 to 254 days (median 66; Lally et al., 2010).
cards.model: Growth that doubles looks like nothing for a long time, then like everything. Don't judge it by week one.
cards.try_today: Draw 30 boxes on paper. Tick one each day you do your tiny habit. Judge it at box 30, not box 3; some habits take longer.
cards.try_team: Everyone secretly picks Pile A or B, then reveal together. Then choose one small daily habit for the group and review it in 30 days.

source.work: Exponential growth bias and household finance (Journal of Finance, 2009); How are habits formed (European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010); Atomic Habits (2018)

cards.hook: The habit isn't too hard. The start is too big. Can you shrink it?
cards.title: The Two-Minute Rule

game.prompt: Is this a good two-minute starting version?

items.text: Read one page of a book
items.why: Tiny, clear, and it often turns into more pages.

items.text: Read 30 pages every night
items.why: Great goal, hard start. Shrink it to one page first.

items.text: Put on your trainers
items.why: Starting is the hard part. Shoes on makes the walk or run likely.

items.text: Run 5 km every morning
items.why: Make the first step the shoes, not the whole run.

items.text: Play one scale on the guitar
items.why: Instrument out, one scale done. Often you keep going.

items.text: Clean your whole room
items.why: Try 'put away one thing' instead. Momentum does the rest.

cards.insight: For many people, starting is the hardest part. Shrink the habit until it's almost silly and the start stops being a battle. A practical rule of thumb, not a lab finding.
cards.model: Make the start so small you can't say no. Master showing up before you improve.
cards.try_today: Take one habit you keep postponing and do only its two-minute version right now. Stopping after is allowed.
cards.try_team: Pick one stalled group task. Shrink it to a 2-minute start (open the doc, list three names, clear one shelf) and do it together right now.

from_source.quote: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; ... the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
from_source.cite: Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 64 (James Legge trans., 1891)
from_source.next_read: Tao Te Ching, ch. 63-64 (on doing great things while they are small)

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); Getting Things Done (2001); Tiny Habits (2019)

cards.hook: People with 'great willpower' may just face fewer temptations. You?
cards.title: Design the Room, Not the Will

questions.q: The things I want to do more (book, water, guitar) are in plain sight.
Starting a good habit takes me under 20 seconds of setup.
Temptations (snacks, games) take effort to reach.
My phone is out of reach when I need to focus or sleep.
The easiest option in front of me (food, apps, plans) is usually a good one.
The people I spend time with do the habits I want.

advice.0: Today's lowest score: visible cues. Put the book on your pillow or the water bottle where you'll see it first.
advice.1: Today's lowest score: friction. Make good habits easier and temptations harder: lay out tomorrow's clothes tonight.
advice.2: Today's lowest score: phone distance. Charge your phone outside the bedroom tonight, or in another room while you focus.
advice.3: Today's lowest score: defaults. Change one: move social apps off your home screen, or put fruit at eye level.
advice.4: Today's lowest score: people. Find one person or group who already does the habit you want, and spend a little time there.

cards.insight: People rating their self-control high reported fewer temptations, not more resisting (Hofmann et al., 2012, correlational). Your surroundings work every day, for free.
cards.model: Make good habits obvious and easy; make bad ones invisible and hard.
cards.try_today: Move one temptation out of sight and put one good cue in plain view. It takes two minutes.
cards.try_team: Walk your shared space (home, classroom, office) for 5 minutes. Each person hides one distraction and puts one good cue in sight.

from_source.quote: Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.
from_source.cite: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 7 'On Crowds' (R. M. Gummere trans., 1917)
from_source.next_read: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 7 'On Crowds'

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); Everyday temptations (J. Personality & Social Psychology, 2012); Good Habits, Bad Habits (2019)

cards.hook: Two neighbouring countries. One tiny box. A gap you won't believe.
cards.title: The Power of Defaults

game.question: In Germany you ticked a box to become an organ donor: about 12% did. In Austria next door, you were a donor unless you ticked a box to opt out. What % were donors there?
game.explain: About 99.98%, effectively everyone (Johnson & Goldstein, 2003). Same kind of choice, different starting setting, and almost nobody changed it. Actual donations differed far less than sign-ups, but opt-out countries still did better.

cards.insight: Most of us keep whatever is already set, because choosing takes effort. So set your own defaults on purpose, and ask who set the others, and for whose benefit.
cards.model: Whatever is already set tends to win. Choose your defaults before they choose for you.
cards.try_today: Change one default now: move one app off your home screen, or leave a book where your phone usually sits.
cards.try_team: List your group's defaults (meeting length, who speaks first, what's in the fridge). Change one this week and see what shifts.

source.work: Do defaults save lives? (Science, 2003); Nudge (2008)

cards.hook: You broke your streak yesterday. What you do next matters more.
cards.title: Come Back Small

steps.scenario: You've walked every evening for 12 days. Yesterday you were exhausted and skipped. Tonight you...

options.text: Do a 5-minute walk, even if it's short.
options.feedback: Yes. A small rep tonight keeps the habit alive. Getting back quickly matters more than the perfect streak.

options.text: Wait until Monday to restart properly.
options.feedback: Understandable, but waiting can turn one miss into a new pattern. A small walk tonight works better.

options.text: Decide you're just not a walking person.
options.feedback: That's a big verdict from one tired day. One miss says nothing about who you are.

steps.scenario: A friend says: 'I missed my practice, so the week is ruined.' You reply...

options.text: Missing once barely matters. What's the smallest bit you could do today?
options.feedback: Kind and practical. You lowered the shame and the bar at the same time.

options.text: You need more discipline.
options.feedback: Well meant, but shame tends to make restarting harder, not easier.

options.text: Yeah, just start fresh next week.
options.feedback: Supportive, but it delays the comeback. Today is a fine day to restart.

cards.insight: William James warned: 'Never suffer an exception to occur' till a habit is rooted. Lally's 2010 data was gentler: one missed day barely slowed habit forming. A miss is an accident.
cards.model: Missing once is an accident. Clear's rule of thumb: come back soon and small, even after two misses or ten.
cards.try_today: Missed something this week? Do its tiniest version today (one page, five push-ups, one minute) and tick it off. That counts.
cards.try_team: Agree on a 'come back small' version of your shared habit (a one-line update instead of the full check-in) for days that fall apart.

from_source.quote: Seize the very first possible opportunity to act on every resolution you make.
from_source.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. IV 'Habit' (third maxim)
from_source.next_read: The Principles of Psychology, ch. IV 'Habit': compare his first three maxims with Lally (2010).

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); How are habits formed (2010); The Principles of Psychology (1890)

cards.hook: You left school or work hours ago. Has your head left yet?
cards.title: Close the Day on Purpose

steps.scenario: It's 10 pm. The class, team or family chat is still buzzing about tomorrow, and nothing can be done about it tonight. You...

options.text: Mute it until morning and pick a set time to catch up.
options.feedback: Nothing changes overnight, and a set catch-up time tells your brain the topic has a place to land.

options.text: Keep checking so you don't miss anything.
options.feedback: Very human, but each check reopens the topic right when you can't act on it. Muting usually costs you nothing.

options.text: Reply to every message so it's all done.
options.feedback: Tidy in theory, but replies invite more replies. The chat rarely ends because you answered it.

steps.scenario: You have an hour before bed and feel drained. Which evening is most likely to leave you rested tomorrow?

options.text: Something absorbing and unrelated: cooking, a walk, a novel, a game with someone.
options.feedback: Right. Studies of mentally 'switching off' after work or study link it to less fatigue the next day.

options.text: Catching up on the news so you're up to date.
options.feedback: Understandable, but news is designed to grab attention, which keeps the mind alert, not settled.

options.text: Going over tomorrow in your head in bed.
options.feedback: Planning is useful, just earlier and on paper. In bed it often turns into replaying, which keeps you awake.

cards.insight: Rest isn't only time off. It's your mind leaving the task too. People who switch off in the evening report less fatigue, though most of this evidence is correlational.
cards.model: An evening only rests you if your mind gets to leave the day too.
cards.try_today: Pick one closing signal for tonight, like muting chats at 9 pm or saying 'done for today' as you shut the bag or laptop.
cards.try_team: Agree on a quiet hour for the group chat (say 9 pm to 7 am), with a clear rule for what counts as truly urgent.

source.work: Sonnentag & Fritz, Journal of Occupational Health Psychology (2007); Wendsche & Lohmann-Haislah, Frontiers in Psychology (2017); Deep Work (2016)

cards.hook: Some 'relaxing' habits wake your brain right up. Spot which.
cards.title: Wind Down or Rev Up?

game.prompt: What does this do to your brain before bed?

items.text: Laying out tomorrow's clothes or bag
items.why: One fewer thing waiting for you in the morning, so one fewer thing to hold in mind.

items.text: One last message check in bed
items.why: It opens new topics at the one moment you can't act on them.

items.text: Replaying an argument to win it this time
items.why: Going over it again keeps the body on alert. Writing it down earlier works better.

items.text: A warm shower or bath an hour or two before bed
items.why: A 2019 review found a warm (about 40 C) bath or shower 1-2 hours before bed helped people fall asleep about 10 minutes sooner.

items.text: Binge-watching a gripping finale until late
items.why: The excitement and the lost sleep time matter as much as the screen's light.

items.text: The same short routine in the same order each night
items.why: Repeated steps become cues: after a while the routine itself signals sleep.

cards.insight: Calm and familiar winds you down. New and exciting revs you up. Sleep helps lock in what you learned (strong evidence). The idea that it also softens bad moods is promising but still debated.
cards.model: Before bed, swap new and exciting for calm and familiar.
cards.try_today: Pick two calm steps (shower, lay out clothes, one page of a book) and do them in the same order tonight.
cards.try_team: As a family or team, swap ideas: each person shares one thing that winds them down and one that secretly revs them up.

source.work: Haghayegh et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews (2019); Diekelmann & Born, The memory function of sleep, Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2010)

cards.hook: One missed day. Does the next thought matter more than the miss?
cards.title: Restart Small, Not Monday

game.prompt: You planned to practise (a sport, an instrument, revision, a run) and skipped it yesterday. Which thought gets you moving again today?
choices: "I've blown it. I'll start properly on Monday."
"Missing once is an accident. A tiny version today."
"I'll do double tomorrow to make up for it."
game.reveal: The second. In Lally's 2010 habit study, missing a single day didn't measurably set people back; the long gap after is the real risk. 'Monday' turns one miss into four. Doubling up sounds keen, but it makes tomorrow feel heavier. Tiny today wins.

cards.insight: A miss is an event, not a verdict about you. Lally's 2010 study found one missed day barely slowed habit forming; the long gap after is the risk. 'Never miss twice' is Clear's rule of thumb.
cards.model: Missing once is an accident. Come back the next day, even if it's tiny.
cards.try_today: Missed something yesterday? Before bed tonight, do its 2-minute version: one page, ten push-ups or one scale. That's the whole task.

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle, How are habits formed (2010)

cards.try_team: When a shared habit slips (a weekly check-in, family dinner), agree a 'tiny version' everyone can do the very next day.

cards.hook: Your resolution died by Tuesday's 1:1. The cue is still alive.
cards.title: Fix the Loop, Not Yourself

game.prompt: Six fixes for meeting habits a manager wants to drop. What is each one relying on?

items.text: Promising yourself you'll stop glancing at messages during 1:1s.
items.why: Trying harder. The buzz still comes and still pays off. Only your effort changed.

items.text: Closing the laptop and putting your phone face down before every 1:1.
items.why: Changing the loop. No buzz in sight means no cue, so there's no urge left to fight.

items.text: Telling yourself to stop jumping in with the answer at stand-up.
items.why: Trying harder. Someone raises a problem (cue) and the old reply fires before you think.

items.text: A stand-up rule for you: ask one question before giving any answer.
items.why: Changing the loop. Same cue, new response. Swapping the action beats trying to block it.

items.text: Vowing to stop answering email at 11 pm.
items.why: Trying harder, at the hour when you're most tired and least likely to stick to it.

items.text: Mail alerts off after 7 pm, and late replies scheduled to send at 8 am.
items.why: Changing the loop. Your cue goes, and your team's 11 pm cue goes with it.

cards.insight: Every right-hand fix hides a cue or swaps a response. The left-hand ones leave the loop intact and rely on effort, which tends to lose on tired, busy days.
cards.model: Don't fight a habit with effort. Find its cue and change one link of the loop.
cards.try_today: Pick the habit that bugs you most in meetings. Write down its cue, then move or hide that cue before your next meeting.
cards.try_team: At stand-up, each person names one team habit to drop (late starts, laptops open). Vote for one, name its cue, change that link for two weeks.

source.work: Wood & Neal, A new look at habits and the habit-goal interface (Psychological Review, 2007); The Power of Habit (2012); Atomic Habits (2018)

cards.hook: No emails after 7. Who's still affected?
cards.title: The Invisible On-Call

game.prompt: Your team rarely gets evening emails, but everyone knows one could arrive and they'd be expected to see it. In one study, that expectation alone was linked to:
choices: More anxiety, but only for staff who actually check
More anxiety for staff, and lower relationship satisfaction for their partners
game.reveal: The last one. In a 2021 study, simply expecting to monitor work email after hours was linked to more anxiety for staff, beyond the time spent on it, and to lower relationship satisfaction for their partners (Becker et al., Journal of Management).

cards.insight: A quiet inbox isn't a closed day. If the rule is 'you might be needed', minds stay on call. Saying when 'off' starts is the team version of a nightly reset.
cards.model: An evening only resets you if 'off' is official. 'Might be needed' keeps everyone on call.
cards.try_today: Pick an 'off' time tonight. Mute work notifications then, and note the one thing that truly couldn't wait (usually nothing).
cards.try_team: Agree one line on when replies aren't expected. Then spend 5 minutes listing what truly can't wait until morning: those get a phone call, everything else waits.

source.work: Killing me softly: Organizational e-mail monitoring expectations' impact on employee and significant other well-being (Journal of Management, 2021)

cards.hook: The learning plan that feels worse is often the one that works.
cards.title: Small Sessions Stack Up

steps.scenario: A test in three weeks (a course exam, a driving theory test, a work certification). You can give it about six hours in total. Which plan leaves the most in your head on the day?

options.text: One big six-hour session the weekend before.
options.feedback: Not the strongest. It feels solid that night, but a lot fades within days. The same hours spread out usually stick better.

options.text: About 35 minutes every couple of days, starting now.
options.feedback: Yes. Spacing is one of the best-replicated findings in learning: each short session tops up what's fading, so it builds on the last.

options.text: Two hours a night for the last three nights.
options.feedback: Better than one marathon, and very common. It's still squeezed late, so there's little time for memories to settle between goes.

steps.scenario: Night before the test. You did the spread-out plan. A friend or colleague crammed all evening and feels sure. You feel shakier. What's most likely?

options.text: You know more than it feels like. Spacing feels harder but tends to last longer.
options.feedback: Right. In one study (learning painters' styles), most people judged cramming as good or better, even though spacing won in their own scores.

options.text: Their way works better after all.
options.feedback: Easy to think, and cramming can get you through tomorrow. But the feeling of 'I know it' is a poor guide to what stays.

options.text: You must have done the plan wrong.
options.feedback: Probably not. Spaced study often feels rusty because you keep meeting things just as you start to forget. That struggle is part of why it works.

cards.insight: Same hours, more stays. Spread-out sessions beat one big push across hundreds of experiments. That's the honest part of '1% a day': each small rep builds on the last.
cards.model: Little and often beats a lot at once. If it feels a bit rusty, it's probably working.
cards.try_today: Pick one topic you'll be tested on. Spend 10 minutes on it now, then book two more 10-minute slots this week.
cards.try_team: Open a weekly meeting or class with 5 minutes: everyone writes what they recall from last week's topic, then checks. No marks, just a top-up.

source.work: Cepeda et al., Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks (Psychological Bulletin, 2006); Kornell & Bjork, Learning concepts and categories (Psychological Science, 2008)

cards.hook: Your group chat is dead on Fridays. What's your first message?
cards.title: Lead With the Why

steps.scenario: You want your friends to start a Friday-night five-a-side (or a study group). In the group chat, your first message is…

options.text: "Pitch at 6, bring £3."
options.feedback: Useful details, but they answer a question nobody has asked yet. Logistics land better once people care.

options.text: "I miss us actually hanging out. Fancy a kickabout on Fridays?"
options.feedback: You gave a reason they can feel: wanting time together. Now the time and the £3 sound like a way in, not a chore.

options.text: "It'll be the best thing anyone's doing this term."
options.feedback: Hype can grab attention, but it doesn't say why it matters to them. A real reason travels further.

steps.scenario: A friend replies: "Sounds good but I'm busy." You reply…

options.text: "Even one week, come for the first half."
options.feedback: You kept the why alive and made the ask smaller. Easy yes, no pressure.

options.text: "Everyone's busy. It's only an hour."
options.feedback: Understandable, but it brushes off their reason. People dig in when they feel unheard.

options.text: "No worries." and leave it there.
options.feedback: Kind and respectful. You could also leave a door open with a smaller, clear option.

cards.insight: Opening with the reason made the details sound like an invitation. Sinek calls it the Golden Circle: why, then how, then what. A handy habit, but his brain-science story isn't backed by research.
cards.model: Say why it matters before what it is. Purpose first, logistics second.
cards.try_today: Before your next request or pitch, write one sentence that starts with "This matters because…" and say that first.

source.work: Start With Why (2009)

cards.try_team: Open your next meeting, class project or family plan with one line each: 'This matters to me because…'. Only then talk times and tasks.

cards.hook: Can a reason that says nothing still get strangers to say yes?
cards.title: The Power of 'Because'

game.prompt: 1978 experiment: someone asks people at a library copier, "May I go first, because I have to make copies?" (An empty reason: everyone in line has to make copies.) How many say yes?
choices: About as many as for a real reason
game.reveal: About as many: 93% said yes, vs 94% for a real reason ("I'm in a rush") and 60% for no reason. But for a bigger ask (20 pages, not 5), the empty 'because' did nothing (24%, same as no reason). Only the real reason helped (42%).

cards.insight: Langer's point was mindlessness: on small asks we react to the word 'because', not the reason. On bigger asks we weigh it. Notice when an empty 'because' works on you. One classic, small study.
cards.model: On autopilot we hear 'because'; awake, we weigh the reason. Give a real one, and listen for real ones.
cards.try_today: Next time you ask someone for something, add 'because…' with your honest reason. Notice how they respond.
cards.try_team: Each person rewrites one request they'll make this week as 'Could we…, because…' with a real reason. Read them aloud: which ones make you want to say yes?

source.work: Langer, Blank & Chanowitz, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1978); Start With Why (2009)

cards.hook: A happy week and a meaningful week: are they the same week?
cards.title: Meaning Lives in the Load

game.prompt: Week A: lie-ins, good food, a film with friends. Week B: tiring, but you helped a friend get ready for a big interview and finished the group project everyone was counting on. Which feels happier, and which more meaningful?
game.reveal: No wrong answer here. In Baumeister's 2013 survey of ~400 US adults, happiness and meaning overlapped a lot. Where they split, happiness went with getting what you need, meaning with giving and caring. A correlation, not a rule, and both count.

cards.insight: Frankl found meaning in what we carry for others. Peterson: pursue what is meaningful, not what is expedient (Rule 7). A heavy week only means something if you can recover from it.
cards.model: Happiness is often about receiving; meaning is often about carrying something worth it.
cards.try_today: Pick one small thing someone relies on you for and do it with care today. Afterwards, notice how it felt.

source.work: Man's Search for Meaning (1946); Baumeister et al., Journal of Positive Psychology (2013); Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (2018)

cards.try_team: Go round the table: each person names one thing others rely on them for that felt heavy but worth it. Notice how often effort and meaning show up together.

cards.hook: Not every weight is yours. Can you tell which ones are?
cards.title: Pick Up the Right Load

game.prompt: Is this a load you can pick up today?

items.text: How you show up for the people who count on you
items.why: Your effort and honesty with them are yours to choose. That's where meaning starts.

items.text: Making everyone like you
items.why: Their feelings aren't yours to control. Your fairness and effort are.

items.text: The mess in your room that's been bugging you
items.why: A small, visible win that's fully yours. Peterson's Rule 6: set your own house in order before you criticize the world. Start in reach, then build.

items.text: Fixing a friend's life for them
items.why: You can support them. Taking over their choices is a weight that crushes both of you.

items.text: Learning the skill your goal actually needs
items.why: Closing your own skill gap is a load that pays you back.

items.text: Every bad thing in the news today
items.why: Caring is good. Carrying it all is not. Pick one thing you can act on instead.

cards.insight: Peterson argues meaning grows from responsibility you choose, starting small and adding more as you get stronger. Epictetus adds the filter: carry only what's in your power. Sort first, then lift.
cards.model: Put down what isn't yours, then pick up one piece of what is, sized for the energy you have today.
cards.try_today: Write down three things weighing on you. Circle the one you can act on, and take one 5-minute step on it.

source.work: Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 6; Epictetus, Enchiridion (c. 125 AD)

cards.try_team: Everyone writes three worries on sticky notes. Sort them together: 'ours to act on' vs 'not ours'. Pick one 'ours' and agree a first step.

from_source.quote: Of things, some are in our power, and others not.
from_source.cite: Epictetus, Enchiridion, ch. 1 (trans. Elizabeth Carter, 1758)
from_source.next_read: Enchiridion, chapters 1-5 (short; about 10 minutes)

cards.hook: Is your life a cage or a flood right now? Find your spot.
cards.title: The Border of Order & Chaos

questions.q: My last two weeks were…

options.label: Different every day, hard to plan

questions.q: How much of the last two weeks was new to me (new tasks, places, people)?
In the last two weeks, how many surprises did you have to absorb?

options.label: A few, and they stretched me
More than I can keep up with

questions.q: My daily routines (sleep, work or homework, phone time) are…
The big things in my life right now (home, work or school, people) feel…

options.label: Several things up in the air at once

zones.label: Leaning Order
zones.text: Today your answers lean toward order: steady, maybe a bit tight. If steadiness is what's helping you recover, that's allowed. When you feel ready, add one small unknown: a new route, a new recipe, one new person.

zones.label: On the Border
zones.text: Today your answers sit on the border: enough structure to stand on, enough new to grow. If some answers sat at opposite ends, pick the one area that feels most out of balance.

zones.label: Leaning Chaos
zones.text: Today your answers lean toward chaos: lots is moving. One fixed anchor helps: same wake time, a daily walk, or a fixed time your phone goes on charge.

cards.insight: Peterson borrows the Taoist image: order is the explored, chaos the unexplored. Too much order goes stale; too much chaos overwhelms. Meaning is found on the border, facing the unknown by choice.
cards.model: Stand on order, then step into the unknown at a pace you choose.
cards.try_today: If you lean Order, try one new thing today. If you lean Chaos, fix one anchor: same bedtime tonight.

source.work: Tao Te Ching, ch. 42; Peterson, Maps of Meaning (1999); 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 2

cards.try_team: Ask the group: which routine keeps us steady, and what one new thing could we try this month? Keep one of each and check back in a week.

from_source.quote: All things leave behind them the Obscurity (out of which they have come), and go forward to embrace the Brightness (into which they have emerged)…
from_source.cite: Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 42 (James Legge trans., 1891)
from_source.next_read: Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 2, the section on order and chaos; then Maps of Meaning (1999), ch. 2

cards.hook: A clown on a unicycle rides past. How many people even notice?
cards.title: What You Focus On Is What You See

game.prompt: You're crossing a campus square, no phone, just walking. A clown in a bright costume rides past on a unicycle. Of people like you, how many noticed?
game.reveal: About half (51%). And of people on a phone call, only about 25% saw the clown, even when asked directly (Hyman et al., 2010). What held their attention, the call, decided what got through.

cards.insight: The missed clown is solid attention science. Peterson's next step, that your aims shape what you notice, is a lens, not a finding. Aristotle's target was the good life; small aims serve it.
cards.model: Your aim is a filter. Change what you're looking for and you'll notice a different world.
cards.try_today: Write one aim for this week in a single line. Tonight, list three things you noticed today that could help it.

source.work: Hyman et al., Did you see the unicycling clown?, Applied Cognitive Psychology (2010); Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I; Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 4

cards.try_team: Everyone writes this week's one aim and swaps papers. For a day, watch out for one thing that could help your partner's aim, then share it.

from_source.quote: Shall we not, like archers who have a mark to aim at, be more likely to hit upon what is right?
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, ch. 2 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1925)
from_source.next_read: Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, chapters 1-2: the chief good as the target of a life

cards.hook: 'Just do your best' sounds kind. Does it actually help you?
cards.title: Aim at a Clear Target

steps.scenario: You want to get fitter this month. Which aim do you write in your phone?

options.text: "Do my best and see how it goes."
options.feedback: Kind and low-pressure. But in many studies, 'do your best' led to less progress than a clear, stretching target. Vague aims are easy to quietly lower.

options.text: "Run 5 km without stopping by the 30th."
options.feedback: Specific, stretching, still reachable. That's the kind of aim goal research keeps backing: you know exactly what you're working toward.

options.text: "Run a marathon by the 30th."
options.feedback: Love the ambition! But goals far beyond reach tend to get dropped, or cause injuries. Stretch, don't snap.

steps.scenario: Plot twist: you've just started chess and know almost nothing. What's your aim for month one?

options.text: "Win 20 online games."
options.feedback: Clear, but on a new, complex skill, chasing results early can backfire: you rush instead of learning. Result targets work better once you know the basics.

options.text: "Learn 3 opening ideas and try them every game."
options.feedback: Smart. When a skill is new and complex, a learning goal (figure out how) tends to beat a result goal. The wins come later.

options.text: "No aim, just play."
options.feedback: Playing for joy is great. If you want to improve, though, one small learning aim gives your practice a direction.

cards.insight: Clear, stretching aims beat 'do your best' in hundreds of studies. Two catches: for new, complex skills, aim to learn first; and over-tight targets can push people to cut corners.
cards.model: Aim specific and a little stretching. If the skill is new, aim to learn first.
cards.try_today: Rewrite one vague aim ('get better at X') as a clear target with a number and a date. Put it where you'll see it.
cards.try_team: Swap 'let's do our best' for one shared target: your team, class or family picks a clear, stretching goal, a date, and how you'll check progress.

from_source.quote: When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
from_source.cite: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 71 (trans. R. M. Gummere, 1920)
from_source.next_read: Seneca, Letter 71, opening paragraphs

source.work: Locke & Latham, American Psychologist (2002); Seijts & Latham, Academy of Management Executive (2005); Seneca, Moral Letters, 71

cards.hook: Bored, stressed, or lost in it? Watch your dot find the zone.
cards.title: Find Your Flow Channel

questions.q: It stretches me.
I could do it half-asleep.
It asks more of me than my usual tasks.
I know how to do most of it well.
I've had little practice at this kind of task.
I've done tasks like this well before.

results.name: Apathy Zone
results.text: Today this task looks low on both challenge and skill: easy to drift and scroll. Pick one tiny goal that stretches you a bit, and start there.

C.name: Anxiety Zone
C.text: Today the task feels bigger than your skill. Shrink it: do one piece you can manage, or get a quick lesson first.

S.name: Boredom Zone
S.text: Today your skill is ahead of the task. Raise the bar: add a time limit, a quality goal, or a harder version.

CS.name: Flow Channel
CS.text: Today high challenge meets high skill. This is where time disappears. Protect it: phone away, one clear goal.

mid.name: On the Fence
mid.text: Today this task sits in the middle on both challenge and skill: not clearly dull, stressful or absorbing. Nudge one side: make it a bit harder, or learn one small piece first.

game.prompt: Think of your main task this week (school, work, a hobby). Answer every line for that task.

cards.insight: People get most absorbed when a high challenge is matched by high skill, a clear goal and quick feedback (Csikszentmihalyi). Too easy bores; too hard stresses. Later studies find the link weaker.
cards.model: Flow = high challenge matched by high skill, a clear goal and quick feedback.
cards.try_today: Pick one task and tweak it: a bit harder if bored, smaller if stressed. Then do 10 minutes with your phone away.

source.work: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience (1990)

cards.try_team: Before a group task, each person rates their part 'too easy', 'just right' or 'too hard'. Swap or split parts until most say 'just right'.

cards.hook: Your last focus session flopped. Which flow ingredient was missing?
cards.title: The Four Flow Ingredients

questions.q: In my last focus session, I knew exactly what 'done' looked like.
In my last focus session, I could tell within minutes if I was on track.
In my last focus session, the task felt neither too easy nor too hard.
In my last focus session, I went 25 minutes without checking my phone.

advice.0: Clear goal scored lowest today. Before you start, write one line: 'Done means…'. Vague goals are a top flow-killer.
advice.1: Quick feedback scored lowest today. Build a check: a practice test, a word count, a friend's quick look. Flow needs to see progress.
advice.2: Right difficulty scored lowest today. Adjust the task: add a challenge if it's dull, split it if it's overwhelming.
advice.3: Interruptions scored lowest today. Put your phone in another room for one 25-minute block. Switching leaves part of your mind elsewhere.

cards.insight: Csikszentmihalyi found flow is more likely with a clear goal, fast feedback and a task just above your skill. Protecting focus from interruptions helps all three. Fix the weakest one first.
cards.model: Don't chase flow. Set up its conditions and let it arrive.
cards.try_today: Fix your weakest ingredient, then work for 10 focused minutes and notice how it felt.

source.work: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience (1990)

cards.try_team: For one 25-minute group work block: agree what 'done' looks like, put all phones away, and check progress together at the end.

cards.hook: Hope is supposed to keep you going. Does it always?
cards.title: Faith Without a Deadline

game.prompt: James Stockdale, a US pilot, was held prisoner in Vietnam for over 7 years. He was asked which fellow prisoners struggled most to hold on. Who did he name?
game.reveal: The optimists. In his telling, they kept picking dates: 'out by Christmas', then Easter. Each missed date hit them harder. Stockdale held two things at once: total faith he'd get home, and zero denial about how bad it was. Hope itself wasn't the problem. Hope pinned to a date he couldn't control was.

cards.insight: This is one man's account to Jim Collins, not a study. Its lesson: hope tied to a date you don't control can break you. Keep faith that you can endure; face today's facts.
cards.model: Keep faith you can get through it. Face the facts honestly. Drop deadlines you don't control.
cards.try_today: Pick a hard thing you're waiting out. Write one honest fact, then one line on what helps you through. Cross out dates you can't control.

source.work: Good to Great (2001), Jim Collins, ch. 4

cards.try_team: Facing a long slog together? List three honest facts on one side and one shared belief about getting through on the other. No promised dates.

cards.hook: Picturing success feels great. That might be the problem.
cards.title: Hope Plus the Wall

steps.scenario: Your exam is in three weeks and you're behind. What do you tell yourself tonight?

options.text: "I'll ace it. Just picture the grade and stay positive."
options.feedback: Feels good, but research suggests pure daydreams can relax you before you've done the work.

options.text: "I want a good grade. My obstacle is my phone, so at 8pm it goes in the kitchen."
options.feedback: A clear wish, the real obstacle, and an if-then plan: hope plus facts.

options.text: "I'm too far behind. It's hopeless."
options.feedback: Honest about today. If success truly feels out of reach, it's worth asking whether this goal, or a smaller one, is the right fight.

steps.scenario: You sprain your ankle just before something you'd been training for. Recovery is slow. Which thought helps most?

options.text: "I'll be back for Saturday."
options.feedback: A hopeful date, but if it slips, the letdown can sap your effort. Hope for the ending, not the date.

options.text: "It'll be slow and some days it'll ache. I'll do my physio daily, and I'll get back."
options.feedback: You name the hard part and still expect to get there. That keeps you doing the physio.

options.text: "It's all ruined, why bother?"
options.feedback: Understandable on a bad day, but it turns a slow fact into a final verdict.

cards.insight: Oettingen's lab work: pairing a wish with its obstacle lifts effort when success feels possible. A related idea: Stockdale, a POW for 7+ years, kept faith yet faced facts (anecdote, via Collins).
cards.model: Wish, then obstacle, then if-then plan. Hope gives the why; facts give the how.
cards.try_today: Name one goal, the biggest inner obstacle, and write one plan: 'If [obstacle], then I will [action].'

source.work: Oettingen, Rethinking Positive Thinking (2014); Collins, Good to Great (2001), ch. 4

cards.try_team: Each person writes the group's goal, the single biggest obstacle, and one 'If..., then we...' plan. Pick the most common obstacle and adopt its plan.

cards.hook: Two people do your exact job. Only one goes home drained. Why?
cards.title: Same Job, Different Aim

game.prompt: Think about your work this week. Pick the answer closest to the truth.

questions.q: Sunday evening, thinking about Monday, I mostly feel…

options.label: Curious what this week moves forward

questions.q: If a new hire asked what my team is for, I'd say…

options.label: Making something easier for specific people

questions.q: My 1:1s mostly cover…

options.label: Where the work is heading and why

questions.q: When a dull task lands on my desk, I…

options.label: Link it to something it makes possible

zones.label: Job-leaning today
zones.text: Today your answers lean 'just a job'. That's a fair deal, not a failing. If the week feels heavy, try naming who one task actually helps.

zones.label: Mixed today
zones.text: Today some of your work points somewhere and some doesn't. Pick the part with no aim and ask your manager, or yourself, what it's for.

zones.label: Aim-leaning today
zones.text: Today your work points at something. Share the aim in your next 1:1 so the team can borrow it, and keep your boundaries: a strong 'why' makes overwork easier to accept.

cards.insight: Even admin assistants with near-identical jobs split into job, career and calling views (Wrzesniewski, 1997). Calling views went with higher satisfaction; correlation, not cause.
cards.model: The task stays the same; the aim you attach to it changes what you notice and what you can endure.
cards.try_today: Write one line above tomorrow's to-do list: 'This matters because it helps ___.' Fill the blank with real people.

source.work: Wrzesniewski et al., Jobs, Careers, and Callings, Journal of Research in Personality (1997); Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (2018)

cards.try_team: At stand-up, each person finishes: 'This week's work helps ___ do ___.' Flag any task nobody can link to a person and ask if it still matters.

cards.hook: Your team has heard the targets ten times. What's still missing?
cards.title: A Face Beats a Slogan

game.question: Fundraising callers spent 5 minutes meeting one student their calls had funded. A month later, how much more money did they raise than callers who didn't?
game.explain: 171% more money and 142% more time on the phone (Grant et al., 2007). Callers who only read a letter from a student didn't improve. Meeting a real person did.

cards.insight: The why that moved callers wasn't a mission statement; it was one person they'd helped. Samples were small, so treat the size as rough. The direction held in Grant's follow-ups.
cards.model: People commit to a why they can picture: a real person helped, not a slogan on a slide.
cards.try_today: Before your next team meeting, find one real message from a customer or user your work helped. Open the meeting with it.

source.work: Grant et al., Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes (2007); Sinek, Start With Why (2009)

cards.try_team: Take 5 minutes: read one real user's message aloud. Each person names one task this week that touches that person, and one that doesn't.

cards.hook: Revision feels like chewing cardboard. Is the fix more willpower?
cards.title: Tune the Task, Not Yourself

steps.scenario: Sunday revision. You've read the same biology notes three times and your brain has left the room. What helps most?

options.text: Read them a fourth time, slower.
options.feedback: Rereading feels productive, but it's too easy to hold your focus. The task is the problem, not you.

options.text: Close the notes and write the 5 key points from memory in 10 minutes.
options.feedback: Now there's a clear goal, a deadline and instant feedback when you check. That's the flow recipe.

options.text: Put a video on in the background to make it less boring.
options.feedback: Fair instinct, boredom is real. But split attention keeps the task too shallow to pull you in.

steps.scenario: Music practice. You've played the same easy piece so many times you're half-asleep and start noodling. What now?

options.text: Play it at a faster tempo, or try it from memory.
options.feedback: Raising the challenge to meet your skill is how boredom turns into focus.

options.text: Keep noodling, it's only practice.
options.feedback: Understandable. You're just spending the session in the boredom zone, where nobody improves much.

options.text: Skip practice next week.
options.feedback: The piece isn't the problem forever; its level is. Change the difficulty before you drop it.

steps.scenario: Maths homework. Three questions in, you're totally stuck, and the group chat is buzzing. What helps?

options.text: Force your way through question 4 anyway.
options.feedback: Brave, but too hard with no feedback feels like stress, not flow. A smaller step gets you further.

options.text: Copy one worked example from the textbook, then try a question just like it.
options.feedback: Shrinking the challenge back to your skill level gets you moving again.

options.text: Answer the chat until you feel like it.
options.feedback: Totally human. The stuck feeling usually waits for you, though; shrinking the task shrinks it.

cards.insight: When 526 US high-schoolers were paged at random through the day, they were most engaged when challenge and skill were both high (Shernoff et al., 2003). Bored isn't lazy; it's a dial.
cards.model: Bored? Make it harder. Stressed? Make it smaller. Then add a clear goal and a quick way to check.
cards.try_today: Turn one dull task into a 10-minute challenge: set a timer, a target number, and a way to check if you hit it.

source.work: Shernoff, Csikszentmihalyi, Schneider & Shernoff, School Psychology Quarterly (2003); Csikszentmihalyi, Flow (1990)

cards.try_team: Revision pairs: each writes a 5-minute recall quiz on a topic for the other, then swap and mark. Make the next quiz harder if someone scored full marks.

cards.hook: You're lost in London. Want the satellite photo or the tube map?
cards.title: The Map Is Not the Territory

game.prompt: You need to get across London fast. You can take one: a perfect satellite photo of every street, or the famous tube map that bends rivers and squashes distances. Which gets you there?
game.reveal: For most trips, the tube map wins. It bends geography on purpose so you can act fast. If you picked the photo, you spotted the catch: studies of London riders found the map's distortions push some people onto slower routes, even riding between stops that are quicker to walk. A map is only good for the trip it was built for.

cards.insight: A more accurate map isn't always a better one. Your beliefs about people, money and yourself are maps too: simplified, useful for some trips, misleading on others.
cards.model: Every belief is a map. Ask 'useful for what?' before asking 'true or false?'
cards.try_today: Pick one firm belief about yourself. Write one situation where that map works and one where it would get you lost.

source.work: Korzybski, Science and Sanity (1933); Box, Science and Statistics (1976) and Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building (1979)

cards.try_team: Each person names one rule your group runs on ('homework before screens', 'we always reply fast'). Ask together: useful for which trip? Where does it mislead?

from_source.quote: All models are wrong but some are useful.
from_source.cite: George E. P. Box, 'Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building' (1979)
from_source.next_read: Box, 'Science and Statistics', Journal of the American Statistical Association 71 (1976), sections 'Parsimony' and 'Worrying Selectively'

cards.hook: Your bathroom scale tells the truth, right? Swipe and see.
cards.title: Map or Territory?

game.prompt: Is this a description, or something you're experiencing directly (still filtered by your senses)?

items.text: The like count on your post
items.why: A tiny slice of who saw it and tapped. It leaves out everyone who smiled and scrolled on.

items.text: The number on your bathroom scale
items.why: A reading of your body, not your body. It ignores muscle, water, and how you feel.

items.text: The rain falling on you right now
items.why: Direct: you can't argue with it, only grab a hood. Even this is your senses' first, thin map.

items.text: A friend's 5-star restaurant review
