items.why: Their compressed experience. Your night there may differ.

items.text: Your 'I'm bad at maths' story
items.why: A summary of some past moments, not a fact about every future one.

items.text: The burn in your legs after running for the bus
items.why: Happening in your body right now. The second you say "my legs are dying", that's already the map.

items.text: Your exam grade
items.why: A useful number that leaves out most of what you actually did.

cards.insight: Most of what we react to is a map: numbers, labels, stories, reviews. Handy, but they leave things out. When a map upsets you, check the territory before you act.
cards.model: When a label stings, ask: is this the thing, or a description of the thing?
cards.try_today: Next time a number or label bothers you today, name one important thing it leaves out.

source.work: Science and Sanity (1933)

cards.try_team: Put one number your group watches on the table (grades, likes, sales, steps). Everyone names one important thing it leaves out. Five minutes, no debate.

cards.hook: Expert doctors scanned for one thing. Guess how many missed a gorilla.
cards.title: You See What You Aim At

game.question: Radiologists searched lung scans for nodules. Researchers pasted in a gorilla 48 times the size of a typical nodule. What % of the radiologists missed it?
game.explain: Drew, Vo & Wolfe (2013): 20 of 24 expert radiologists (83%) missed it, even though eye-tracking showed most of those who missed it looked right at it. Their aim was 'find nodules'.

cards.insight: Attention follows aims. Even experts hunting for one thing filter out much of the rest, a gorilla included. That's how focus works, but it means your goals quietly shape what you see.
cards.model: Your aim is a filter. Change what you're looking for and you'll notice a different world.
cards.try_today: Before your next walk or meeting, set a new aim: 'notice three things that are going well.' Then count them.

source.work: Drew, Vo & Wolfe, The invisible gorilla strikes again, Psychological Science (2013)

cards.try_team: Before a class, practice or meeting, give everyone a different 'look for' job: one good idea, one risk, one person who's quiet. Compare notes at the end.

from_source.quote: My experience is what I agree to attend to. Only those items which I notice shape my mind.
from_source.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. XI 'Attention'
from_source.next_read: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 1, ch. XI 'Attention', opening pages (free online)

cards.hook: A stranger swaps into someone else mid-chat. How many notice?
cards.title: The Person Swap

game.prompt: A stranger with a map asks you for directions. As you explain, two workers carry a door between you. Behind it, the stranger is replaced by a different person with different clothes and voice. Would you notice?
game.reveal: If you said yes, you're in good company: almost everyone does. But in Simons and Levin's 1998 street study, about half of the people kept giving directions to the new person without noticing. One likely reason: people stored a rough label ('a stranger with a map'), not the face. In a follow-up, students noticed a swap more often when the stranger looked like a fellow student.

cards.insight: We often store a rough label, not the details. A small study (15 people), but this 'change blindness' has been found many times.
cards.model: We often store a label, not the person. Aim to notice the person and you'll see more of them.
cards.try_today: In your next chat, set a tiny aim: notice one thing about the person (their mood, their eyes, what they care about today).
cards.try_team: Pair up for 60 seconds of chat, then turn back to back. Each changes one small thing (glasses, sleeve, hair). Turn round: who spots it? Then swap.

source.work: Simons & Levin, Failure to detect changes to people during a real-world interaction, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (1998)

cards.hook: 11pm. A text: 'We need to talk.' What does your gut say?
cards.title: Reframing

steps.scenario: 11pm. Your best mate (or your partner, or your boss) texts: 'We need to talk. Tomorrow?' No context. Your heart speeds up. What do you tell yourself?

options.text: 'I've done something wrong. I should prepare for the worst.'
options.feedback: A very normal first reaction, especially if you're already on edge. It's just one story out of many, and you don't have to settle it tonight.

options.text: 'I don't know what this is yet. Could be news, a favour, a plan. I'll find out tomorrow.'
options.feedback: That's reappraisal: same facts, wider frame. You haven't lied to yourself, you've just stopped writing the ending early.

options.text: 'Whatever, I don't care.'
options.feedback: Pushing the feeling down often keeps it buzzing underneath. Research suggests suppression tends to work worse than reframing.

steps.scenario: Next morning, still a bit nervous. What's a useful move?

options.text: Reply: 'Sure. Anything I should prepare? What time works?'
options.feedback: Turns a vague threat into a concrete plan. Often you'll get the context you were missing.

options.text: Replay worst cases until you meet
options.feedback: Understandable, but going round in circles rarely adds information. One small action usually helps more.

cards.insight: Events arrive inside a frame. Changing the frame, not the facts, can change your body's reaction and your next move. Studies find reappraisal usually beats pushing feelings down.
cards.model: Same facts, new frame: 'What else could this mean?' is the cheapest stress tool you own.
cards.try_today: When something stings today, write two other honest explanations for it before you react.

source.work: Gross & John, Individual differences in two emotion regulation processes (2003); Epictetus, Enchiridion; Seneca, Moral Letters 13

cards.try_team: If you lead a team or class: before sending 'Can we talk?', add one line of context ('Nothing bad, want to plan next week'). Agree this as a group rule.

from_source.quote: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
from_source.cite: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 13 'On Groundless Fears', trans. R. M. Gummere (1917)
from_source.next_read: Seneca, Moral Letters, Letter 13 'On Groundless Fears' (about 4 pages)

cards.hook: Some 'positive thinking' makes you feel worse. Can you spot which?
cards.title: Reframe, Not Spin

game.prompt: Something went wrong. Is this thought an honest reframe, or spin?

items.text: Failed your driving test: 'Now I know exactly which two things to practise.'
items.why: True, useful, and it points to a next step. That's a reframe.

items.text: Failed your driving test: 'Who cares, I never wanted to drive anyway.'
items.why: Sour grapes. If part of you doesn't believe it, it won't calm you.

items.text: Friend hasn't replied all day: 'She might just be busy. I'll check in tomorrow.'
items.why: A believable other explanation, plus an action. You stay open, not certain.

items.text: Low mark on an essay: 'Grades are meaningless, so it doesn't matter.'
items.why: Denial. Grades leave things out, but this one still has information for you.

items.text: Bus cancelled, 25-minute wait: 'Good time to call Grandma.'
items.why: Same facts, better use of them. Nothing here is pretend.

items.text: Feeling low: repeating 'I am totally happy and loved' ten times.
items.why: In one study, statements like this made people with low self-esteem feel worse.

cards.insight: Reframing works when you believe the new frame. Spin and forced positivity can backfire: in one study, 'I am a lovable person' made people with low self-esteem feel worse.
cards.model: A good reframe is true, believable and points to a next step. If it's not true, it's spin.
cards.try_today: When something stings today, write one reframe. Then ask: do I actually believe this? If not, find a truer one.
cards.try_team: Someone shares a small setback. Everyone offers one reframe; the group votes each 'honest' or 'spin', and says why. Keep it light and kind.

source.work: Gross & John (2003); Wood, Perunovic & Lee, Positive self-statements: Power for some, peril for others, Psychological Science (2009); Epictetus, Enchiridion

from_source.quote: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things.
from_source.cite: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5, trans. George Long
from_source.next_read: Epictetus, Enchiridion, sections 1-5 (about two pages)

cards.hook: Your heart's pounding before a big talk. Enemy or fuel?
cards.title: Stress Mindset

questions.q: Before an exam or big moment, my racing heart means…
Feeling stressed before something important…

options.label: Gets in the way of doing well

questions.q: In general, the effect of stress on me is…
When I notice stress building, I usually…

options.label: Avoid the task until it passes
Calm it a little, then use the energy on the task

zones.label: Leaning 'stress harms'
zones.text: Today your answers read stress mostly as danger, and if you've had a hard time, that makes sense. For everyday nerves (a talk, an exam), try one more reading: my body is getting me ready. If stress feels constant or heavy, that's a reason to get support, not a mindset failure.

zones.label: A mixed lens
zones.text: Today your answers see both sides. Next time, notice which story you pick in the moment. Sometimes you can pick which story to lean on.

zones.label: Leaning 'stress can fuel'
zones.text: Today your answers read stress as energy. Keep that, and still watch for real overload: rest is part of the deal.

cards.insight: In Alia Crum's studies, seeing stress as enhancing went with somewhat better work and fewer symptoms. Reading a racing heart as 'gearing up' helped too. Effects are modest; heavy stress needs support.
cards.model: Some stress is your body gearing up, not breaking. Reframe the everyday kind; get support for the heavy kind.
cards.try_today: Before your next nervous moment, take one slow breath and tell yourself: 'This is energy for something I care about.'

source.work: Crum, Salovey & Achor, Rethinking stress (2013); Jamieson et al., Journal of Experimental Psychology: General (2012); McGonigal, The Upside of Stress (2015)

cards.try_team: Before a match, exam or big deadline, everyone says one thing they care about in it. Then together: 'This buzz is energy for that.' One slow breath.

cards.hook: 'I'm just not a people person.' How would you prove that?
cards.title: Pragmatic Truth

game.prompt: You reckon you're 'not a people person'. What's the best way to actually find out?
choices: Think back over every awkward chat you've had
Ask three friends whether they agree
For one week, start one short chat a day and see how each goes
game.reveal: Memories and friends' views are filtered through the belief itself, and beliefs like this steer you away from the moments that would test them. Peirce said an idea's meaning lies in its practical effects; James went further: its truth is worked out in experience. So act as if it might be false, and watch.

cards.insight: Pragmatism asks: what happens when you act on this idea? A lens, not a lab finding, and facts still matter. James's view of truth was hotly disputed (Russell among others); use it as a method.
cards.model: Judge a belief by its consequences: run the experiment, then decide.
cards.try_today: Pick one limiting belief. Try one small, low-stakes action that only makes sense if it's false. Note what happened, no grading.

source.work: James, Pragmatism (1907); Peirce, How to Make Our Ideas Clear (1878)

cards.try_team: Each person names one 'we're just not the kind of group that…' belief. Pick one, design a one-week test that could prove it false, and agree when to check.

from_source.quote: The truth of an idea is not a stagnant property inherent in it. Truth happens to an idea.
from_source.cite: William James, Pragmatism (1907), Lecture VI 'Pragmatism's Conception of Truth'
from_source.next_read: James, Pragmatism, Lecture II 'What Pragmatism Means', then Lecture VI (free online)

cards.hook: Notice, interpret, adjust: which step do you use least?
cards.title: Your Perception Loop

questions.q: I notice details others miss, including small signs things are changing.
Changes around me often catch me by surprise when others saw them coming.
When something goes wrong, I can come up with more than one explanation.
My first read of a situation usually feels like the only one.
When I'm proven wrong, I update my view fairly quickly.
I keep doing what I've always done, even when results disappoint.

results.name: All three dimmed today
results.text: Today no step stands out, which often happens when we're tired or busy. A starting point, not a verdict. Begin with Notice: one minute a day spotting three new things.

P.name: Noticing leads today
P.text: Today you rate your noticing highest, with less room for second readings or changing course. Try asking 'what else could this mean?'

A.name: Interpreting leads today
A.text: Today you rate yourself strong at re-reading situations, but you may be working from thin data and slow to change course. Gather one more fact before deciding.

R.name: Adjusting leads today
R.text: Today you rate yourself quick to change course. Check you're adjusting to real signals, not noise: notice and interpret first.

AP.name: Noticing + interpreting
AP.text: Today you rate yourself clear-seeing and flexible, but insight may not turn into change. Try Adjust: make one small change this week.

PR.name: Noticing + adjusting
PR.text: Today you rate yourself quick to spot change and move, maybe on the first reading. Try Interpret: pause for a second explanation.

AR.name: Interpreting + adjusting
AR.text: Today you rate yourself good at reframing and adapting, but you may be missing inputs. Try Notice: ask someone what they see that you don't.

APR.name: All three switched on
APR.text: Today you rate all three steps as switched on. Keep it honest by checking results, not just feelings. Practise the step you scored lowest; if two tie, start with Adjust.

mid.name: Evenly balanced today
mid.text: Every step scored near the middle. Start with Adjust: name one thing you've kept doing this month even though results disappointed, and change one detail of it this week.

cards.insight: Qlip's own framework, built on Powers's control theory, not a tested scale: notice, interpret, adjust, then act again. The step you use least is a good one to practise.
cards.model: Notice, interpret, adjust. Practise the step you use least.
cards.try_today: Take one frustrating situation from this week and run it through the step you use least, on paper, in five minutes.

source.work: Qlip's house model (a notice-interpret-adjust loop), drawing on Powers, Behavior: The Control of Perception (1973)

cards.try_team: Take one recent hiccup (a lost match, a missed deadline, a row). Spend 90 seconds each on: what did we see, what did it mean, what will we adjust?

cards.hook: A thermostat is smarter than most New Year's resolutions. Why?
cards.title: Perceive, Adjust, Repeat

steps.scenario: You promised yourself 20 minutes of guitar (or running, or a language app) a day. Two weeks in, you've done it 3 times. What would a thermostat do?

options.text: Try harder tomorrow. More willpower.
options.feedback: Very common, and it rarely changes the result. A thermostat doesn't try harder; it checks the reading and adjusts.

options.text: Admit it's just not for me and stop.
options.feedback: Maybe, one day. But you'd be quitting on 3 data points without asking why. Check first, then decide.

options.text: Look at what actually happened on the missed days, change one thing, try again.
options.feedback: That's the loop: perceive, appraise, recalibrate, act, check. Small corrections beat big resolutions.

options.text: Write a bigger, more perfect plan.
options.feedback: Tempting, but a new plan without new information repeats the old one. Measure first.

steps.scenario: You check: the missed days were all when you got home after 8pm. Best adjustment?

options.text: Move practice to before dinner, and make it 10 minutes on late days.
options.feedback: Adjust to the real signal, keep it small, then check again next week.

options.text: Promise to do 40 minutes on the good days to make up.
options.feedback: Ambitious, but it ignores the signal. The late days will still break the loop.

cards.insight: Good controllers don't need a perfect plan. They need a fast loop: notice, compare, adjust, act, check. Habits and goals improve the same way: small corrections, often.
cards.model: Don't aim for a perfect plan. Aim for a fast, honest feedback loop.
cards.try_today: Pick one goal. Set a 2-minute check-in tonight: what happened, what does it mean, what will I adjust tomorrow?
cards.try_team: End a practice, lesson or week with 3 questions, one minute each: What happened? What does it mean for our goal? What one thing do we change next time?

source.work: Powers, Behavior: The Control of Perception (1973); adapted as Qlip's notice-interpret-adjust loop (house model)

cards.hook: You walk in wearing something cringe. How many people clock it?
cards.title: Fewer People Notice Than You Think

game.question: Students put on a T-shirt with a big, uncool singer's face and walked into a room of peers. What % of the room later noticed who was on the shirt?
game.explain: About 23%. The shirt-wearers guessed close to half would notice (Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, 2000). Guessed high? So did they: you feel your own shirt all day; others mostly don't.

cards.insight: We sit at the centre of our own story, so we guess others are watching us about twice as closely as they are. Small studies, but the pattern has held up.
cards.model: You're the star of your show, an extra in everyone else's. Halve your guess of who noticed.
cards.try_today: Felt everyone saw a slip? Write your guess of who noticed. Then ask one person you trust, or just see if anyone mentions it tomorrow.

source.work: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, 'The Spotlight Effect in Social Judgment', JPSP (2000)

cards.try_team: Everyone writes one moment this week they felt watched (a wrong answer, a typo, a stumble). Others say if they even noticed. Usually: barely.

cards.hook: One awkward moment. How long will people remember it?
cards.title: The Slip Is Smaller Outside Your Head

steps.scenario: In class you answer a question confidently, and it's wrong. A couple of people laugh. Next lesson, you…

options.text: Say 'oops, mixed that up' if it comes up, and put your hand up again
options.feedback: A light, quick fix tells people it's no big deal, and it usually isn't to them.

options.text: Stay silent for the rest of term so it can't happen again
options.feedback: Understandable, it stung. But the silence costs you more than the slip did; most classmates likely moved on that day.

options.text: Explain at length why your answer was nearly right
options.feedback: Natural urge, but a long defence keeps the moment alive. Short and light lets it fade.

steps.scenario: You lose your words mid-sentence while speaking to a group at work or in a club meeting. Afterwards you…

options.text: Replay it all evening and plan to avoid speaking up
options.feedback: Very common. But people judge our public mishaps less harshly than we expect (Savitsky, Epley & Gilovich, 2001).

options.text: Note one thing to tweak next time, then let it go
options.feedback: Yes. Others mostly remember your point, not the pause. One fix, then move on.

options.text: Send everyone a message apologising for the stumble
options.feedback: Kind instinct, but it puts a spotlight on something few people noticed.

steps.scenario: At a family get-together you call a relative's partner by the wrong name. You…

options.text: Smile, say 'sorry, got my names muddled', and carry on
options.feedback: Right. A warm one-line fix is what most people hope for, and then they move on.

options.text: Avoid them for the rest of the day
options.feedback: Easy to feel that pull. But steering clear makes the moment bigger than the slip was.

options.text: Bring it up again later to apologise once more
options.feedback: Caring, but one apology is enough; repeating it keeps the spotlight on.

cards.insight: Your slip feels huge because you see it from the inside. Others are busy with their own day, and judge it more gently than you predict. A quick, light fix is usually enough.
cards.model: A quick, light fix ends the moment for them; replaying it only keeps it going for you.
cards.try_today: Next time a cringe moment replays, write one line: how a kind friend who was there would describe it. Then close the note.

source.work: Savitsky, Epley & Gilovich, 'Do Others Judge Us as Harshly as We Think?', JPSP (2001)

cards.try_team: Before a talk or meeting, agree a light line for slips ('let me try that again'). Use it once on purpose so it feels normal for everyone.

cards.hook: Lottery winners vs their neighbours. Who's happier a year on?
cards.title: The Thrill Wears Off

game.prompt: Researchers asked big lottery winners, up to about 18 months after winning, how happy they felt day to day. Compared with their neighbours, they were…
game.reveal: About the same, in a small 1978 study of 22 winners (Brickman et al.), and they enjoyed small things like a chat or a joke a bit less. Picked 'happier'? You're partly right: a large Swedish study found big winners stayed more satisfied with life for years, though not happier from moment to moment (Lindqvist et al., 2020).

cards.insight: New things quickly become your normal, so the daily glow fades even when the gain is real. How satisfied you feel with life can shift; the day-to-day buzz mostly settles back.
cards.model: Gains turn into the new normal. Expect the glow to fade and plan for it.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you were excited to get last year. Use it today as if it were new, and notice one detail you'd stopped seeing.

source.work: Brickman, Coates & Janoff-Bulman, JPSP (1978); Lindqvist, Östling & Cesarini, Review of Economic Studies (2020)

cards.try_team: Each person names something they wanted badly that now feels ordinary. Then name one way to make it feel fresh again. Share the best idea.

cards.hook: Some changes you get used to in weeks. Others never feel normal.
cards.title: What You Get Used To

game.prompt: Does the feeling fade, or does it stick around?
game.right: Keeps its effect (you don't fully adapt)

items.text: The buzz of a brand-new phone
items.why: Within weeks it's just your phone. Same features, far less thrill.

items.text: The money from your first Saturday job
items.why: Soon it's just normal money and your wants rise to match.

items.text: Getting the bigger bedroom
items.why: A week later it's just your room.

items.text: Finally getting the trainers you saved up for
items.why: A few weeks in they're just your trainers. The saving-up was half the buzz.

items.text: A 50-minute bus to college or work every day
items.why: Some studies found long commuters less satisfied even years later (Stutzer & Frey, 2008), though later data are mixed.

items.text: Seeing friends in new, varied ways each week
items.why: Varied, surprising joys seem to keep their effect longer than fixed ones (Lyubomirsky, 2011), though this is less directly tested.

cards.insight: We adapt fast to stable gains, slowly to daily hassles and changing joys. So cutting daily friction and keeping good things varied tends to pay off longer than more stuff.
cards.model: Expect stable gains to fade. Cutting daily hassles and keeping good things varied tends to last longer.
cards.try_today: Name one daily hassle you've 'accepted'. Spend 10 minutes finding one way to shrink it this week.

source.work: Lyubomirsky, 'Hedonic Adaptation to Positive and Negative Experiences' (2011); Stutzer & Frey, 'Stress that Doesn't Pay: The Commuting Paradox' (2008)

cards.try_team: List the group's three biggest daily hassles and three recent 'upgrades'. Vote: which fix would still feel good in six months?

cards.hook: Butterflies before you go on. Calm down, or call it excitement?
cards.title: Call It Excitement

steps.scenario: Five minutes before you sing at a friend's party (or give a toast, or take a penalty), your stomach is flipping. What do you tell yourself?

options.text: 'Calm down. Just calm down.'
options.feedback: Very natural. But buzzing to calm is a big jump, and it often doesn't stick. There's a shorter one.

options.text: 'I'm excited.'
options.feedback: Yes. Nerves and excitement feel alike in the body. Calling it excitement is a smaller jump, and in small studies it helped people perform.

options.text: 'Don't think about it.'
options.feedback: Understandable. Pushing a feeling away tends to keep it buzzing underneath.

steps.scenario: A deadline is tomorrow (homework, a form, a work report) and you've hit a snag. Your chest is tight. What's the useful next move?

options.text: Name it ('this is pressure, it means I care'), then pick one step you can do in 20 minutes.
options.feedback: Yes. The feeling stays, but now it's pointed at a task, not at you.

options.text: Tell yourself you're useless under pressure.
options.feedback: A harsh story on top of a hard moment. It's one reading, not a fact, and it drains energy you need.

options.text: Push through all night with no break.
options.feedback: Sometimes needed, but even fuel needs rest. Running on empty tends to make snags bigger.

cards.insight: Nervous and excited feel alike in the body. In Alison Wood Brooks's small studies, saying 'I'm excited' helped singing and speaking more than 'calm down'. Effects were modest.
cards.model: Don't fight the buzz. Rename it: 'I'm excited' points the energy at the task.
cards.try_today: Before your next nervous moment, say 'I'm excited' out loud, then name the first small thing you'll do.

source.work: Brooks, Get excited: Reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General (2014)

cards.try_team: Before a match, test or launch, each person names the part they're nervous about, adds 'and I'm excited about it', then you agree step one together.

cards.hook: Every status report says green. So why is your best engineer so quiet?
cards.title: The Dashboard Is a Map

steps.scenario: Friday dashboard: every ticket closed on time, sprint all green. In your 1:1, Priya, your strongest engineer, says she's 'fine', but she's stopped speaking up in stand-ups. What do you trust?

options.text: The dashboard. Numbers don't have moods.
options.feedback: Not quite. Numbers feel solid after a long week, but this one only counts tickets. It was never built to see energy, doubts or workarounds.

options.text: Neither yet. Ask her: 'What isn't the dashboard showing me this week?'
options.feedback: Yes. The report is the map; Priya is standing in the territory. Ask her what's missing from it, then decide.

options.text: Priya. Dashboards always lie.
options.feedback: Close, but too far. The numbers are true about what they count. The fix is to add a second view, not to bin the map.

steps.scenario: Your director wants a new target: 15 tickets closed per person per week, reviewed monthly. What's the most likely side effect?

options.text: Tickets get split smaller and the hard, messy work gets pushed back.
options.feedback: Right. That's Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes a target, people steer the number, not the work. Pair it with a check on quality.

options.text: Output rises across the board.
options.feedback: Possible for a while, and a fair hope. But when praise rides on a count, people learn to move the count, often faster than the work.

options.text: Nothing changes; it's just a number.
options.feedback: Understandable, but targets exist to change behaviour. The real question is which behaviour they reward.

cards.insight: Verdict: the dashboard was true and still misleading. A metric is a map of the work, not the work. Turn it into a target and people start steering the map.
cards.model: Every number is a map: ask what it can't see, and never let one number be the whole target.
cards.try_today: Pick one metric you report. Write one thing it can't show, then ask one person on your team about exactly that.

source.work: Goodhart, Problems of Monetary Management: The U.K. Experience (1975); Campbell, Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change (1979); Strathern, 'Improving ratings' (1997)

cards.try_team: 5 min: list your team's top 3 metrics. For each, everyone writes how they could hit it while making the work worse. Add one counter-check.

cards.hook: Angry client, live call. Mask it or reframe it: which costs more?
cards.title: Reframe, Don't Just Mask

game.prompt: A client tears apart your team's work for ten minutes on a call. Option A: keep a straight face and push the anger down. Option B: tell yourself "they're under launch pressure, this is fear talking". Which one makes you forget more of what they asked for?
game.reveal: Pushing it down. In lab studies, people told to hide their feelings remembered fewer details of what they had just seen and heard. People who reframed did not pay that memory cost (Richards & Gross, 2000). Hiding takes effort, and the effort comes out of your attention.

cards.insight: Verdict: masking isn't free; it spends attention you need for the details. Reframing keeps your memory working. Lab evidence, not yet tested on real client calls.
cards.model: Don't just mask it, re-read it: 'What else could explain this?' keeps your head in the room.
cards.try_today: Before your next tough meeting, write one generous reason for the hardest person's behaviour. Re-read it if things heat up.

source.work: Richards & Gross, Emotion regulation and memory: The cognitive costs of keeping one's cool, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2000)

cards.try_team: 5 min: each person shares this week's spikiest client or stakeholder message. The team suggests two non-hostile reasons for it, then drafts the reply.

cards.hook: Same page, same night. Your mate remembers stuff you never even saw.
cards.title: Read Like a Burglar

steps.scenario: English class. Everyone reads the same short story: two boys skip school and hang out at one boy's house. Half the class is told to read it as a burglar, half as someone buying the house. Who remembers the coin collection and the TV?

options.text: The 'burglars'
options.feedback: Yes. In the original study, readers recalled more of the details that mattered to their role. Your goal quietly decides what sticks.

options.text: Everyone the same. It's the same words.
options.feedback: Fair guess, it literally is the same text. But goals changed what stuck: burglars kept the valuables, buyers kept the house's faults.

options.text: The buyers, they'd read more carefully
options.feedback: Nice thinking, but no. Buyers remembered buyer stuff, like a leaky roof, and let more of the valuables slip.

steps.scenario: The night before something you need to be ready for (a test, a driving theory exam, a briefing at work). You've got 20 minutes and your notes. Which is the burglar move?

options.text: Read the notes twice and highlight the important bits.
options.feedback: Not the strongest move, though most of us do it. 'Important' isn't a goal, so everything starts looking highlightable.

options.text: Write 3 questions you think will come up, then read hunting for the answers.
options.feedback: Yes. You've given your eyes a job. Research on pre-questions suggests it mostly boosts what you asked about, so pick good ones.

options.text: Watch a summary video at double speed.
options.feedback: Quick, and sometimes useful. But watching without a question is browsing: you catch what's loud, not what's tested.

cards.insight: Verdict: you never just read a page, you read it for something. Give your attention a job and it grabs the details that fit it, and skips the rest.
cards.model: Your goal is a search filter: set it before you look, or something else will set it for you.
cards.try_today: Before your next reading (revision notes, a report, a contract), write one question at the top of the page. Read only to answer it.

source.work: Pichert & Anderson, Taking different perspectives on a story, Journal of Educational Psychology (1977); Carpenter & Toftness, The effect of prequestions on learning from video presentations, JARMAC (2017)

cards.try_team: Study group or team, 5 min: everyone reads the same page in a different role (examiner, sceptic, newcomer). Share what each role noticed.

cards.hook: Snowball or thermostat? Sort 6 everyday loops.
cards.title: Snowball or Thermostat?

game.prompt: Does this settle back like a thermostat (←) or keep growing like a snowball (→)?

items.text: Short on sleep, you scroll late to unwind, then sleep even less
items.why: Tired leads to scrolling leads to more tired. Vicious circles are reinforcing too.

items.text: Money in savings earns interest, which earns more interest
items.why: Growth feeds more growth. Classic reinforcing loop.

items.text: You feel hungry, eat, and the hunger goes away
items.why: Your body pulls you back toward a set point. That's balancing.

items.text: A rumor spreads: the more people know, the more people tell
items.why: Each new teller makes more tellers, whether the rumor is true or false.

items.text: You speed up when late, slow down once you're on time
items.why: The gap to a goal drives the action, and the action closes the gap.

items.text: Practicing makes it easier, so you practice more
items.why: Virtuous circle: skill makes practice pleasant, practice builds skill.

cards.insight: Snowball loops amplify, good or bad. Thermostat loops pull back to a target. It's a thinking tool from systems science, not a lab finding. Know which loop you're in before you push.
cards.model: Reinforcing loops snowball; balancing loops hold a set point. Ask which one is running.
cards.try_today: Write one habit you want as a loop: 'A makes B, B makes more A.' Find the arrow you can strengthen today.

source.work: Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008)

cards.try_team: With your team, class or family: each person names one loop in your shared life. Vote: snowball or thermostat? Pick one to feed or break this week.

cards.hook: One skipped walk can turn into a lost month. Where would you cut it?
cards.title: Cut the Vicious Circle

steps.scenario: The loop: low energy, so you skip your walk. Moving less, you sleep a bit worse. Worse sleep, even less energy. Which link is easiest to cut today?

options.text: Fix my energy first, then start walking again
options.feedback: Waiting to feel ready is how the loop keeps running. Energy often follows movement, not the other way round.

options.text: A 5-minute walk, even feeling flat
options.feedback: Yes. Tiny and doable on a bad day. One small action can turn the same circle the other way.

options.text: Plan a full new fitness routine for Monday
options.feedback: Big plans feel good, but they start later and ask for energy you don't have yet.

steps.scenario: A week later the loop is turning the good way, then you miss two days. You think…

options.text: "Ruined. Back to square one."
options.feedback: Understandable, but loops don't reset to zero. Calling it ruined is what restarts the downward lap.

options.text: "Two days off. Short walk today and the loop keeps turning."
options.feedback: Right. A loop is about direction, not a perfect streak. Nudge it back the good way.

cards.insight: Spirals can feel like bad luck or a flaw in you, but often they're just a loop. Draw the circle and you see each link. You don't fix it all, just one arrow.
cards.model: If it keeps getting worse (or better) on its own, look for the circle, then cut or feed one link.
cards.try_today: Sketch one loop in your life as 4 boxes and arrows. Circle the easiest link and change just that one today.
cards.try_team: Draw a loop your group keeps falling into (late starts, messy kitchen, missed homework). Everyone marks the easiest link. Change that one for a week.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990)

cards.hook: Why do you always end up scalding, then freezing, in a new shower?
cards.title: The Shower Problem

steps.scenario: Hotel shower. Water is cold. You turn the knob toward hot. Five seconds later it's still cold. You…

options.text: Crank it much hotter. It clearly isn't working.
options.feedback: Very human, and exactly how you get scalded. The hot water was already in the pipe, on its way.

options.text: Wait a few more seconds before touching it again
options.feedback: Yes. The pipe adds a delay. Give your last action time to show its result.

options.text: Give up and take a cold shower
options.feedback: Brave, but the system was working. It was just slow to report back.

steps.scenario: Three weeks into a new workout plan, you don't feel much different yet. You…

options.text: Double the intensity to force results
options.feedback: That's the shower move again. Overcorrecting raises the risk of injury or burnout.

options.text: Keep the plan and judge it again after 8 weeks
options.feedback: Bodies, skills, and relationships all respond with a lag. Set a fair review date.

options.text: Switch to a totally different plan
options.feedback: Switching resets the clock before the first plan could show anything.

cards.insight: When results lag behind actions, it feels like nothing works, so we push harder. Then the late results land and we overshoot. Many problems are delay problems, not effort problems.
cards.model: Slow feedback plus impatience equals overshoot. Act, wait for the lag, then adjust.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you're trying to improve. Write how long it fairly takes to show results, and set a reminder for that date.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Sterman, Business Dynamics (2000)

cards.try_team: Before changing a plan, ask the group: how long should this take to show results? Agree a review date and don't touch the knob before it.

from_source.quote: Faster is slower.
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4, then ch. 5 'A Shift of Mind' on balancing loops and delays

cards.hook: You text "??" three times, then 4 replies land at once. Same bug.
cards.title: The Beer Game

game.prompt: A shop orders from a factory, and deliveries take weeks. Shoppers go from buying 4 boxes a week to 8, then stay at 8. What do the shop's orders do?
choices: Orders rise smoothly to 8 and stay there
Orders swing between huge and almost none
game.reveal: They swing wildly. Stock is slow to arrive, so players keep ordering, then drown in it and stop. If you picked 'smoothly', that's what nearly everyone expects. Afterwards, many blamed wild customer demand. It had changed once. Same bug as your three "??" texts: acting again before the first one has landed.

cards.insight: In MIT's Beer Game, played since the 1960s, smart people make the same swings again and again. The cause isn't who plays. It's the delay built into the chain.
cards.model: When everyone overreacts, look for the delay before you look for someone to blame.
cards.try_today: Sent a message or made a request? Wait for it to land before you send it again.
cards.try_team: When a problem in your group swings back and forth, draw the chain on paper and mark every delay. Agree to change one thing at a time.

source.work: Sterman, 'Modeling Managerial Behavior: Misperceptions of Feedback in a Dynamic Decision Making Experiment', Management Science (1989); Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990)

from_source.quote: Structure influences behavior.
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 3 'Prisoners of the System, or Prisoners of Our Own Thinking?'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 3 (the full Beer Game story and its three lessons)

cards.hook: Most people push where change is hardest. Can you find the lever?
cards.title: Where to Push

game.prompt: You want to stop doomscrolling at night. Rank these fixes from weakest to strongest lever.
items: Numbers: 10 fewer minutes a night
Information: a screen-time report of your real hours
Rules: phone charges outside your bedroom
Goals: judge nights by how rested you feel
Mindset: scrolling stops feeling like rest
game.explain: 1 Numbers: easy to change, rarely sticks. 2 Information: you see the real cost. 3 Rules: the setup does the work. 4 Goals: redefine a good night. 5 Mindset: changes what you want. Meadows ranked 12 such levers.

cards.insight: Adjusting numbers rarely changes how a system behaves. Changing who sees what, the rules, or the goal moves more with less force. Meadows called her list a draft, not a law.
cards.model: Numbers are easy and weak. Information, rules, and goals are harder and strong.
cards.try_today: Pick one stuck problem. Instead of 'more' or 'less' of something, write one change to its rules, information, or goal.

source.work: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999)

cards.try_team: At your next meeting, class council or family talk, ask 'what are we actually rewarded for?' before asking anyone to try harder.

from_source.quote: Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth.
from_source.cite: Archimedes, as reported by Pappus of Alexandria, Collection, Book 8 (traditional English rendering)
from_source.next_read: Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 6 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System', especially her warning that leverage points are counterintuitive

cards.hook: When stuck, do you try harder or change the game? Find out.
cards.title: Tweaker or Redesigner?

questions.q: You keep spending too much. Your first move is…

options.label: Promise to be stricter with myself
Track every purchase for a month
Make savings move automatically on payday

questions.q: Your group project keeps missing deadlines. You…

options.label: Make progress visible to everyone each week
Ask what each person is really rewarded for

questions.q: You want to read more. You…

options.label: Put a book where your phone usually sits
Just try to remember to read

questions.q: The same argument with a friend, sibling or partner keeps coming back. You…

options.label: Prepare my points better for next time
Agree a pause rule when it starts
Ask what each of you is actually trying to protect

zones.label: Tweaker
zones.text: Today's answers reach for effort and numbers first. Honest work, but tiring. Next time, ask: what rule, information, or goal is producing this?

zones.label: Switch-hitter
zones.text: Today's answers switch between pushing harder and redesigning. Notice which one you grab under stress, and try the redesign first once this week.

zones.label: Redesigner
zones.text: Today's answers look for the structure behind the problem. Keep going, and give redesigns time: their results also arrive late.

cards.insight: Meadows ranked 'numbers' (targets, budgets) among the weakest levers; we add willpower to that list. Changing what people see, what's rewarded, or the goal tends to work with less strain.
cards.model: Before pushing harder, ask what structure is producing the result.
cards.try_today: Take one 'I should try harder' and rewrite it as a change to your surroundings, rules, or reminders. Do that change now.

source.work: Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008)

cards.try_team: Next time your team or class is stuck, ban 'try harder' for 5 minutes. List changes to what people see, what's rewarded, or the goal.

from_source.quote: Small changes can produce big results
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4; then Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 6

cards.hook: A city paid people per rat tail. Guess what it got more of.
cards.title: The Rat Tail Bounty

game.prompt: Hanoi, 1902. Rats are spreading through the new sewers, so officials pay a small bounty for every rat tail handed in. What happens next?
game.reveal: It backfired. People were seen with live rats missing only their tails, so the rats kept breeding, and there were reports of rats being farmed for tails. Historian Michael Vann documented it. If you guessed 'rats disappear', that's what the officials expected too: the fix rewarded tails, not fewer rats.

cards.insight: A quick fix eases the symptom today, while its side effect quietly feeds the problem. The side effect is late, so the fix looks like it works, and we repeat it.
cards.model: Ask of every fix: what does this reward, and what will it feed in three months?
cards.try_today: Name one quick fix you use often (snacking, cramming, avoiding). Write what it might be feeding in the long run.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Vann, 'Of Rats, Rice, and Race' (2003)

cards.try_team: Pick one rule or reward your group uses (points, chores, targets). Spend 5 minutes asking: how could someone game this, and what would that feed?

from_source.quote: Today's problems come from yesterday's "solutions."
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4; Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 5 'System Traps... and Opportunities'

cards.hook: The fix worked on Monday. Why is the problem bigger by Friday?
cards.title: Spot the Backfire

steps.scenario: You sleep until noon on Sunday to catch up after a late Saturday. What's the hidden side effect?

options.text: None, you've paid back the sleep
options.feedback: You do get rest. But your body clock also shifts later, and that bill arrives on Sunday night.

options.text: Sunday night you can't fall asleep, so Monday hurts
options.feedback: Right. The lie-in eases today's tiredness and pushes your clock later. Researchers call the mismatch 'social jet lag'.

steps.scenario: Homework's due in an hour (or a work task you don't really get), so you copy a mate's answers. What grows?

options.text: Nothing, it's handed in
options.feedback: Real relief tonight. But the gap in what you understand keeps growing underneath.

options.text: The bit you don't understand, which shows up in the test
options.feedback: Yes. The fix ends tonight's panic and feeds next month's.

steps.scenario: Plot twist from real life: Mexico City, 1989. To cut smog, each car is banned from driving one weekday, based on its number plate. What did many families do?

options.text: Took the bus on their banned day
options.feedback: That was the plan. But a cheaper way round it was sitting in the used-car market.

options.text: Bought a second car, often an older one
options.feedback: Yes. Car numbers rose, many extra cars were old and dirtier, and economist Lucas Davis found no clear drop in air pollution.

options.text: Drove less on every day of the week
options.feedback: A hopeful guess. The rule only touched one day, so it changed which car, not how much driving.

cards.insight: Every fix has a main effect and a side effect. The main effect shows up fast; the side effect arrives later and often feeds the problem you were fixing.
cards.model: Before a quick fix, ask: what will this feed when no one is watching?
cards.try_today: Take one fix you used this week (lie-in, snack, cramming). Write its side effect and one tweak that keeps the relief.
cards.try_team: Before agreeing a new rule at home, school or work, take 5 minutes: each person imagines how a clever lazy person would get round it.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Davis, 'The Effect of Driving Restrictions on Air Quality in Mexico City', Journal of Political Economy (2008); Wittmann, Dinich, Merrow & Roenneberg, 'Social Jetlag', Chronobiology International (2006)

from_source.quote: Behavior grows better before it grows worse.
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4, then Appendix 2 on the 'Fixes That Fail' archetype

cards.hook: What's your crutch quietly doing to the muscle underneath?
cards.title: Crutch or Muscle?

game.prompt: Does this treat the symptom, or build the real capacity?

items.text: A third coffee every afternoon to get through the slump
items.why: It works today, but it can hurt tonight's sleep, which deepens tomorrow's slump.

items.text: Moving bedtime 20 minutes earlier
items.why: If short sleep is behind the slump, this goes after the cause, not the feeling.

items.text: Always getting a parent or friend to make your awkward phone calls
items.why: Relief now, but your own skill and confidence never get the reps.

items.text: Making the awkward call yourself, with them nearby for backup
items.why: Uncomfortable, but each try builds the skill you were avoiding.

items.text: Using autocorrect for a word you never learn to spell
items.why: Harmless here. Not every crutch is bad; just know which muscle you're skipping.

items.text: Asking a teacher to explain the step you keep getting wrong
items.why: Help that teaches is the opposite of a crutch: it shrinks your need for help.

cards.insight: When a quick fix keeps solving a problem for you, your own ability can weaken, so you need the fix more. Help isn't the issue; help that replaces learning is.
cards.model: Use help that teaches. Watch for fixes you need more each month.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you always outsource or avoid. Do one small piece of it yourself today, with support nearby if you need it.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990)

cards.try_team: Each person names one task they always hand to the same helper. Pair up: the helper coaches, the other does it, once this week.

from_source.quote: The easy way out usually leads back in.
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 5, the trap 'Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor'

cards.hook: A group can know more than any member. Does it use what it knows?
cards.title: The Clue Nobody Said

game.prompt: Researchers gave small groups facts about three candidates in a student election. Together each group knew enough to spot the strongest one, but the key facts were split up, a piece per person. What did most groups do?
choices: Pooled the clues and picked the best
Talked about what they all already knew
game.reveal: They mostly talked about what they all already knew. In Stasser and Titus's 1985 study, shared facts got far more airtime than facts only one person held, so few groups picked the best candidate. When everyone got all the facts up front, most did. If you guessed 'pooled the clues', you're in good company: that's what most people expect groups to do.

cards.insight: Groups drift to facts everyone already holds, so the clue only one person has can go unsaid. Being quiet isn't the fix on its own; asking for unshared facts is.
cards.model: Before a group decides, ask: what does only one of us know?
cards.try_today: In your next family, class or work chat about a decision, ask: 'Has anyone noticed something the rest of us haven't?' Then wait.
cards.try_team: Before deciding, each person writes one fact they think only they know. Read them all aloud first, then discuss. Five minutes.

source.work: Stasser & Titus, 'Pooling of Unshared Information in Group Decision Making', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1985); Cain, Quiet (2012)

cards.hook: The first voice sets the room. How do you hear the slower ones?
cards.title: Make Room for Slow Thinking

steps.scenario: A teacher asks the class a hard question. Three hands shoot up within a second. What gets more thoughtful answers from more students?

options.text: Call on the first hand to keep things moving
options.feedback: Quick and natural. But then the fastest few do the thinking, and the rest learn they needn't.

options.text: Wait about three silent seconds before calling on anyone
options.feedback: Yes. In Mary Budd Rowe's classroom studies, waiting about 3 seconds led to longer answers and more students joining in.

options.text: Give the answer so nobody feels stuck
options.feedback: Kind, but it skips the thinking. A few seconds of quiet is often all people need.

steps.scenario: Your team or club needs ideas to stop wasting time. The usual way is everyone talking at once. What tends to give more ideas?

options.text: An open brainstorm, loudest ideas first
options.feedback: Lively, but people wait their turn and drop ideas while others talk.

options.text: Everyone writes ideas alone for 5 minutes, then shares
options.feedback: Yes. Diehl and Stroebe (1987) found people working alone, then pooling, had more ideas than groups brainstorming aloud. Waiting your turn blocks ideas.

options.text: Let the most senior person decide quickly
options.feedback: Fast, but you get one view of a problem everyone sees a part of.

steps.scenario: Your group chat (friends, team or family) keeps flaring up into fall-outs. Everyone has a quick theory why. What finds the real pattern?

options.text: Go with whoever's loudest
options.feedback: Loud isn't proof. A pattern that repeats needs the record more than a debate.

options.text: Scroll back and look at when each fall-out actually started
options.feedback: Yes. A pattern hides in any one argument and shows up when you line them up.

options.text: Mute the chat and start a new one
options.feedback: Tempting, but the same pattern usually moves to the new chat with you.

cards.insight: Loud, fast rooms reward the first idea. A short pause, silent writing or a look back at the record lets slower clues surface. That helps everyone think, not just quiet people.
cards.model: Pause before the talk: silence, paper or a look back lets slow patterns show.
cards.try_today: Next time you ask someone a question, count three seconds in your head before you fill the silence.
cards.try_team: Open your next meeting, class or family plan with 3 minutes of silent writing. Go round, one idea each, before open talk.

source.work: Rowe, 'Wait Time: Slowing Down May Be a Way of Speeding Up!', Journal of Teacher Education (1986); Diehl & Stroebe, 'Productivity Loss in Brainstorming Groups: Toward the Solution of a Riddle', JPSP (1987); Cain, Quiet (2012)

cards.hook: You're helping a struggling hire. Could the help be the problem?
cards.title: The Set-Up-to-Fail Loop

game.prompt: A new hire misses one deadline. You start checking their work and ask for daily updates. Six weeks on, what tends to happen?
choices: They play it safe, take less initiative, and slip more
game.reveal: Often the second. Manzoni & Barsoux called it the set-up-to-fail syndrome: close checking signals doubt, the person pulls back, and the boss reads that as proof. If you picked 'improve', that's the hope behind most checking. Both sides feed the loop, usually with good intentions.

cards.insight: Your doubt and their doubt feed each other in a snowball loop. Neither person is the villain; the circle is. Cut one arrow: name the worry and agree a clear way back.
cards.model: Treating someone like they'll fail can help them fail. Look for the loop before you judge the person.
cards.try_today: Pick the person you worry about most. In your next 1:1, ask 'What would help you own this?' and agree a date to stop checking in.
cards.try_team: In stand-up, each person names one task where they'd like less checking and one where they'd like more. Agree one change each; review in two weeks.

source.work: Manzoni & Barsoux, 'The Set-Up-to-Fail Syndrome', Harvard Business Review (1998)

cards.hook: Your team hit the deadline. Will next month pay for it?
cards.title: The Six-Week Bill

game.prompt: Six weeks later, does this fix hold or bite back?

items.text: The whole team works weekends to hit a launch date
items.why: Bites back as a habit: tired people make more errors, and fixing them eats next month. Once is fine.

items.text: Adding two new people to a project that's already late
items.why: Bites back: veterans stop to train them. Brooks saw this make late projects later.

items.text: Muting an alert that keeps going off
items.why: Bites back: quiet today, surprise later. The cause is still there, now unwatched.

items.text: A big discount to hit this quarter's sales target
items.why: Bites back: clients learn to wait for the discount, so next quarter starts weaker.

items.text: Spending a day finding why the same handover keeps failing
items.why: Holds: slower this week, but the problem stops coming back.

items.text: A one-page checklist for the step everyone forgets
items.why: Holds: cheap, and it fixes the cause (memory) rather than the symptom.

cards.insight: Four of six bite back. Quick fixes ease the symptom now; the bill lands weeks later, so no one links the two. Repenning & Sterman saw whole teams stuck firefighting this way.
cards.model: Before a quick fix, ask: what will this cost in six weeks, and who will pay?
cards.try_today: Pick one fix your team keeps repeating. Spend 20 minutes asking 'why does this keep happening?' until you hit a cause you can change.
cards.try_team: List three fixes from last month on a whiteboard. Everyone writes what each one cost later. Pick one to swap for a root-cause fix this sprint.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Repenning & Sterman, 'Nobody Ever Gets Credit for Fixing Problems that Never Happened', California Management Review (2001); Brooks, The Mythical Man-Month (1975)

cards.hook: New school, two months in, no real mate yet. Broken, or just early?
cards.title: Friendship Runs on a Delay

game.question: Roughly how many hours of hanging out does it take to turn someone you know into an actual friend?
game.explain: About 90 hours, by one study's estimate: around 50 for a casual friend, 200+ for a close one (Hall, 2019, surveys of adults and university students). Time chatting and joking counted more than sitting in the same lesson.

cards.insight: Two months of lessons might be only 10 hours of real talk. Friendship has a long delay, so 'nothing's happening' usually means 'not enough hours yet', not 'something's wrong with me'.
cards.model: When results lag effort, count the hours you've put in, not the weeks on the calendar.
cards.try_today: Pick one person you get on with and add 20 minutes of real hanging out: walk home together, share lunch, or play one game.
cards.try_team: Class or club: pair up with someone you barely know and swap three fun questions for 5 minutes. Repeat weekly so the hours add up.

source.work: Hall, 'How many hours does it take to make a friend?', Journal of Social and Personal Relationships (2019)

cards.hook: A bat and ball cost 1.10. Your gut already has an answer. Check it.
cards.title: Fast & Slow Thinking

game.question: A bat and a ball cost 1.10 together. The bat costs 1.00 more than the ball. How much is the ball, in cents?
game.explain: If the ball were 10, the bat would be 1.10 and the total 1.20. Ball 0.05 + bat 1.05 = 1.10. Most people's first answer is 10, including many students at top universities.

cards.insight: The 10-cent answer arrives instantly and feels right. That's your fast mind. The slow mind only checks when you ask it to. Clever people miss this too; a pause is what helps.
cards.model: Fast thinking proposes, slow thinking checks. When it feels obvious and matters, check once.
cards.try_today: Say your gut answer out loud before your next decision that matters, then ask: 'How would I check this?'

source.work: Cognitive Reflection and Decision Making (2005); Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

cards.try_team: Give everyone the bat-and-ball puzzle on paper, answers written silently. Reveal, then ask: which of our choices feel this obvious but never get checked?

cards.hook: Hare or owl: who's actually making your decisions this week?
cards.title: Who's Driving: Hare or Owl?

questions.q: A message from your boss or teacher annoys you. You usually…
Someone proposes a big change in a group chat (team, class, family). You…

options.label: Ask for a quick call before deciding

questions.q: When a headline makes you angry, you…

options.label: Check who else reports it before sharing

questions.q: Someone asks how long a task will take you (a work job, a project). You…

options.label: Say you'll reply after breaking it down

zones.label: Hare-led
zones.text: Today your answers lean fast. That's efficient for routine stuff. For the few choices that matter, add one deliberate pause.

zones.label: Shared driving
zones.text: Today your answers switch between speeds. The skill now is noticing which moments deserve the owl.

zones.label: Owl-led
zones.text: Today your answers lean slow. Useful for big calls, costly for small ones. Watch for overthinking small, reversible choices; the hare handles those well.

cards.insight: Neither speed is better. The fast mind slips on numbers, anger and new things. 'System 1 and 2' (Stanovich & West, 2000) is a metaphor, not two brain parts.
cards.model: Let the hare handle the routine; call the owl for anything costly, emotional, or new.
cards.try_today: Pick one trigger (an annoying message, a snap estimate) and make it your rule to wait 10 minutes first.

source.work: Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

cards.try_team: In your next planning or group chat, agree one 'owl rule': no estimate or reply to a heated message without one question first. Review in a week.

cards.hook: First, a number unrelated to the answer. Watch it bend your guess.
cards.title: Anchoring

game.question: What percentage of UN member countries are in Africa?
game.explain: 54 of the 193 UN members are African: about 28%. Before you guessed, you saw 65. We can't know if it moved your guess, but on average it moves people: in the 1974 study, people who saw a wheel land on 65 guessed a median of 45%, and those who saw 10 guessed 25%.

cards.insight: An irrelevant number still drags your guess toward it. Price tags like 'was 199, now 99' use this. Knowing about it helps a little; bringing your own number helps more.
cards.model: The first number sets the field. Bring your own number before you hear theirs.
cards.try_today: Next time you sell something online, haggle at a market or talk pay, write your price and one reason it's fair before you see their offer.

source.work: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974)

cards.try_team: Before your friends or team guess a number together (trip cost, queue time, a deadline), everyone types their guess in the chat at the same time.

cards.hook: Your brain ranks dangers by how easily they come to mind. Test it.
cards.title: Availability Bias

game.prompt: Most people's gut sense of how often this happens is…

items.text: Dying in a plane crash
items.why: Crashes get huge coverage. Per mile, commercial flying is far safer than driving.

items.text: Being killed by a shark
items.why: About 5 to 10 unprovoked shark deaths a year worldwide.

items.text: Getting hurt cycling or walking near traffic
items.why: Road injuries are the top killer of 5 to 29-year-olds worldwide (WHO). So routine they're rarely news.

items.text: A child taken by a total stranger
items.why: Stranger abductions are very rare; most missing children are runaways or family cases.

items.text: Heart disease as a cause of death
items.why: It's the top cause of death worldwide (WHO), yet rarely makes headlines.

items.text: Diabetes as a cause of death
items.why: It kills over a million people a year worldwide (WHO), quietly and with little coverage.

cards.insight: Vivid, dramatic events are easy to recall, so they feel common; slow, ordinary risks hide. Guesses also drift toward the middle. Your feed is a highlight reel, not a map of risk.
cards.model: Easy to imagine is not the same as likely. Ask for the count, not the story.
cards.try_today: Look up one number the next time a scary story grabs you: how many times a year does this actually happen?

source.work: Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability (1973)

cards.try_team: Everyone names the danger they worry about most. Look up one real yearly number for each together. Which fears shrink, and which grow?

cards.hook: 2, 4, 6 follows a secret rule. Most people's first guess is wrong.
cards.title: Confirmation Bias

steps.scenario: The numbers 2-4-6 follow a hidden rule. You can test any three numbers and learn if they fit. Your hunch: 'even numbers going up by 2.' Which test teaches you the most?

options.feedback: It fits, but it would fit your hunch either way. You'd learn nothing new. This is what most people try.
Another yes, but again only a test your hunch already predicts. Confirming feels productive; it rarely is.
Yes! Your hunch says 'no'. If it fits, your hunch is wrong. That's a real test. Spoiler: it fits.

options.text: Just guess the rule now
options.feedback: Bold! But without a test that could prove you wrong, you'd be guessing blind.

steps.scenario: 1-2-3 fits. So does 3-17-90. 6-4-2 does not. What's the rule?

options.text: Any three numbers going up
options.feedback: Correct. In Wason's 1960 study, only about 1 in 5 people named it on their first try, mostly because they only tested examples they expected to fit.

options.text: Numbers with a pattern
options.feedback: Close in spirit, but 3-17-90 has no neat pattern. Simpler: they just go up.

options.text: Even numbers only
options.feedback: 1-2-3 fit, so odd numbers are allowed. The rule is broader: any rising sequence.

cards.insight: We often test ideas in ways that can only say 'yes'. It feels like proof but isn't. Researchers debate how irrational this is; the fix is clear: seek what could prove you wrong.
cards.model: Don't ask 'what fits my idea?' Ask 'what would I see if I were wrong?'
cards.try_today: Pick one belief you hold firmly. Write down one thing that, if you saw it, would change your mind. Go look for it.

source.work: On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task (1960)

cards.try_team: Play 2-4-6: one person holds a secret rule, others test triples aloud. Afterwards count how many tests could have gotten a 'no'.

from_source.quote: The human understanding when it has once adopted an opinion ... draws all things else to support and agree with it.
from_source.cite: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (1620), Book I, Aphorism 46 (trans. Spedding, Ellis & Heath)
from_source.next_read: Novum Organum, Book I, Aphorisms 45–52 (the 'Idols of the Tribe')

cards.hook: In an argument, are you defending a fort or drawing a map?
cards.title: Soldier or Scout?

questions.q: Someone shares a study that disagrees with you. First thought:

options.label: Look for what's wrong with it, but not what's right
Check its methods, the same way I'd check one I agreed with
Read what they found before judging

questions.q: When did you last change your mind on something you cared about?
Your feed mostly shows people who…

options.label: I follow some smart critics on purpose

questions.q: Being proven wrong feels like…

zones.label: Soldier mode
zones.text: Today's answers lean toward defending, which is very human. Try treating one belief as a draft, not a fort.

zones.label: Switching
zones.text: Today's answers mix scouting and defending. Notice which topics made you defensive; that's where your map is least checked.

zones.label: Scout mode
zones.text: Today's answers lean curious about being wrong. Keep it kind: scouts share maps, they don't sneer at others' wrong turns.

cards.insight: Everyone slips into defending. Scouting isn't caring less; it's wanting an accurate map more than wanting to be right. Your answers are a snapshot, not a verdict.
cards.model: A soldier asks 'Can I believe this?' or 'Must I believe this?' A scout asks 'Is it true?'
cards.try_today: In your next disagreement, ask one honest question: 'What would change your mind?' Then answer it yourself too.

source.work: The Scout Mindset (2021)

cards.try_team: In your next group debate, each side must state the other side's best argument first, until the other side says 'yes, that's it'.

cards.hook: Heads you win £15. Tails you lose £10. Flip?
cards.title: Loss Aversion

game.prompt: One fair coin flip, real money. Heads: you win £15. Tails: you lose £10. On average you come out £2.50 up. Do you take it?
game.reveal: Most people say no. There's no wrong answer: it's your money. But notice the pull. In Kahneman's studies people wanted a win about twice the loss before they'd flip. Losses tend to feel roughly 1.5–2.5× as strong as equal gains.

cards.insight: Saying no is fine when the loss would really hurt. But we often skip small, smart risks just because losing stings. Some research finds the effect smaller than claimed for small amounts.
cards.model: Losses shout, gains whisper. For small, repeatable bets, judge the average, not the sting.
cards.try_today: Name one small, reversible bet you've avoided (a new routine, asking for help, delegating a task). Write the worst case and your plan B.

source.work: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk (1979)

cards.try_team: Each person writes one small risk they've avoided. Swap papers, estimate the realistic worst case for each other, then ask: what would help if it happened?

from_source.quote: We suffer more ... when we fall from a better to a worse situation, than we ever enjoy when we rise ...
from_source.cite: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (6th ed., 1790), Part VI, Section I
from_source.next_read: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part VI, Section I, 'Of the Character of the Individual, so far as it affects his own Happiness'

cards.hook: Same mug, same room. Just being handed it changes its price.
cards.title: The Endowment Effect

game.question: Students got a free mug. Those who got one named a selling price; those who didn't named a buying price. How many times more did owners want?
game.explain: About 2.5×. In Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler's 1990 study, owners asked a median of about $7.12 and buyers offered about $2.87. Same mug. Just being handed it made giving it up feel like a loss.

cards.insight: Owning something makes letting go feel like losing, so we overprice our stuff. The effect is real but its size depends on the setup; some studies find it much smaller.
cards.model: Ask 'Would I buy this today, at this price?' not 'How much would losing it hurt?'
cards.try_today: Look at one thing you're selling online or keeping in your wardrobe or garage: would you buy it today at that price?
cards.try_team: Ask everyone: name one thing we keep only because we already have it (a tool, a habit, a club, a routine). Would we choose it again today?

source.work: Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem (1990); Plott & Zeiler (2005)

cards.hook: Stuck on how to succeed? Ask how you'd fail instead.
cards.title: Inversion

steps.scenario: Your goal: be a better friend this year. Which question gets you a useful answer fastest?

options.text: How could I be the perfect friend?
options.feedback: Nice aim, but 'perfect' gives vague answers like 'be there more'. Hard to act on.

options.text: What would make sure I lose my friends?
options.feedback: Yes. Failure is easy to picture: cancel last minute, only talk about me, forget birthdays. Concrete and fixable.

options.text: What do the experts say friendship is?
options.feedback: Useful later, but it's about friendship in general, not your habits. Inversion goes straight to yours.

steps.scenario: Your list: cancel last minute, only talk about yourself, never ask questions, forget birthdays. Best next move?

options.text: Fix all four starting tomorrow
options.feedback: Big energy! But four changes at once rarely stick. Start with one.

options.text: Circle the one you already do a little, and stop it this week
options.feedback: Exactly. Small, honest, doable. Removing one quiet mistake often beats adding a big new effort.

options.text: Feel bad about the list
options.feedback: Very human, but guilt doesn't change much. The list is a map, not a verdict. Pick one item.

cards.insight: Picturing failure gives a checklist; success stays vague. Imagining an outcome had already happened helped people find more reasons for it (Mitchell et al., 1989). Klein's premortem builds on it.
cards.model: Ask what would guarantee failure, then don't do that.
cards.try_today: Pick one goal. Write 3 ways it could go wrong. Circle the easiest to avoid and skip it today. It's a checklist, not a verdict on you.

source.work: Poor Charlie's Almanack (2005); Mitchell, Russo & Pennington, Back to the Future: Temporal Perspective in the Explanation of Events (1989)

cards.try_team: Ask the group: 'How could we make this trip, project or term a total disaster?' List ideas for 5 minutes, then pick one to prevent.

from_source.quote: Invert, always invert.
from_source.cite: Carl Jacobi, as quoted by Charlie Munger, Harvard School commencement speech (1986)
from_source.next_read: Charlie Munger's 1986 Harvard School commencement speech on prescriptions for misery, reprinted in Poor Charlie's Almanack

cards.hook: A city paid for every rat tail. Guess what it got more of.
cards.title: Second-Order Thinking

steps.scenario: Hanoi, 1902. Rats are spreading through the new sewers, so French officials pay a bounty for every rat tail handed in. What happens next?

options.text: The rat problem shrinks
options.feedback: That's the first-order guess, and it's what officials expected. The records show a twist.

options.text: People cut off tails, let the rats go, and some breed them
options.feedback: Yes. Tailless rats were soon seen in the streets, and officials later found rat farms. The bounty paid for tails, not for fewer rats.

options.text: Nobody bothers to catch rats
options.feedback: The opposite. Tails poured in by the thousand, just not in a way that helped.

steps.scenario: Your school gives a merit for every homework handed in on time. Ask 'and then what?' twice. What's the sneaky side effect?

options.text: Everyone learns more
options.feedback: That's the first-order hope. Ask 'and then what?' once more: what does the merit actually reward?

options.text: People rush rubbish homework just to hit the deadline
options.feedback: Yes. The merit counts 'on time', not 'good', so some people hand in fast, thin work. A quick quality check would keep the reward honest.

options.text: Nobody hands anything in
options.feedback: Unlikely. Rewards usually do change behaviour, just not always the way the rule-maker hoped.

cards.insight: First-order asks 'what now?' Second-order asks 'and then what?' Historian Michael Vann documented Hanoi's 1902 rat-tail bounty; the famous Delhi cobra version has thin records.
cards.model: Every fix creates new incentives. Ask 'and then what?' at least twice.
cards.try_today: Before you set yourself a rule or reward (screen time, streaks, revision points), write 'and then what?' and answer it twice.

source.work: The Most Important Thing (2011); Der Kobra-Effekt (2001); Vann, Of Rats, Rice, and Race (French Colonial History, 2003)

cards.try_team: Before your group sets a target (streaks, pages read, sales calls), ask: 'How could someone hit this number without actually doing the thing?'

from_source.quote: We can never do merely one thing.
from_source.cite: Garrett Hardin, 'The Cybernetics of Competition', Perspectives in Biology and Medicine (1963)
from_source.next_read: Frédéric Bastiat, That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen (1850), Chapter 1, 'The Broken Window' (public domain)

cards.hook: A test says you have a rare condition. How worried should you be?
cards.title: Base Rates

game.question: A condition affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test catches every real case but gives a false positive to 5% of healthy people. You test positive. Chance you have it?
game.explain: Of 1,000 people: 1 truly has it. About 50 healthy people also test positive. So 1 of ~51 positives is real: about 2%. In a 1978 Harvard study, 27 of 60 doctors and students answered 95%; only 11 got about 2%.

cards.insight: When something is rare, most positives are false alarms. That's why doctors confirm with a second test. This is just the math; real results need a real doctor.
cards.model: Start with how common it is, then adjust for the new evidence. Rare things stay fairly rare.
cards.try_today: Ask 'Out of 1,000 similar cases, how many usually turn out this way?' the next time a story or alarm surprises you.

source.work: Interpretation by Physicians of Clinical Laboratory Results (1978)

cards.try_team: Turn one scary claim into counts together: 'Out of 1,000 people like this, how many…?' Sketch the 1,000 as dots if it helps.

from_source.quote: A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.
from_source.cite: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section X, Part I
from_source.next_read: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, 'Of Miracles', Part I

cards.hook: One sentence about a stranger. Your gut picks a job in a second.
cards.title: The Count Beats the Story

game.prompt: Steve is a man in the USA. He's shy, tidy, loves order and small details, and is happiest with a quiet book. Is Steve more likely a librarian or a farmer?
game.reveal: Librarian is the natural pick: the story fits. But Kahneman notes the US had over 20 male farmers for every male librarian. Unless that description is more than 20 times likelier for a librarian, which few descriptions are, farmer is the better bet.

cards.insight: A vivid description makes us forget how common each option is. Kahneman and Tversky showed this in 1973. Thinking in counts ('out of 100 men like Steve…') makes the error shrink.
cards.model: The story says who fits. The count says who's common. Start from the count, then let the story adjust it.
cards.try_today: Next time you judge someone or something from one detail, ask: 'How common is each option in general?' before you decide.
cards.try_team: Before judging a new idea, person or rumour from one story, ask the group: 'How often does this usually happen?' Find one real number together.

source.work: On the Psychology of Prediction (1973); Judgment under Uncertainty (1974); Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), Introduction; Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995)

cards.hook: You watched for one minute. You're already sure who's smarter.
cards.title: The Quizmaster Illusion

game.prompt: A coin toss splits two people. One writes 10 hard trivia questions from their own odd knowledge. The other must answer them and gets about 4 right. Based on this, who is actually more knowledgeable?
game.reveal: You can't tell: the coin set the roles. Asking your own questions is easy; answering someone else's is hard. Yet in Ross's 1977 study, watchers rated the questioner more knowledgeable, and so did the people answering.

cards.insight: We see the person, not the setup that made them look good or bad. Even knowing the roles were random didn't stop the bias.
cards.model: Before judging the player, look at the role they were handed.
cards.try_today: Next time someone looks clueless (a new classmate, colleague or relative), ask: 'Whose home turf is this?' before you judge them.
cards.try_team: Swap roles for 5 minutes: the newest person explains their own speciality and the expert asks questions. Notice who suddenly looks 'smart'.

source.work: Social Roles, Social Control, and Biases in Social-Perception Processes (1977)

cards.hook: Someone lets you down. Your brain writes their whole biography.
cards.title: Blaming People, Not Situations
